item.title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
item.description: Greece as a place to invest, compared with the EU on investment, bond yields, debt, wages, electricity, the state, the courts and logistics with Eurostat data.
item.content:encoded:
Greece as a place to invest, compared with the EU on investment, bond yields, debt, wages, electricity, the state, the courts and logistics with Eurostat data.

What is this?

Is Greece a good place to invest? The answer depends on the investor, whether they buy Greek bonds, build a factory or open a business, but some questions matter to all of them, and each can be measured in the same way for every EU country:

  1. Do investors invest in Greece? What the economy invests, and what comes from abroad.
  2. Is the country a financial risk? The interest rate on its bonds, and its debt.
  3. What does it cost to produce there? Wages and electricity.
  4. How well does the state work? Bureaucracy, regulation, the rule of law and corruption.
  5. Do the courts protect investors? How long a case takes, and what companies think.
  6. Can goods move? Ports, roads and customs.

The data come from Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU, and from the World Bank, and are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures. Two sets of figures come from the European Commission’s 2026 EU Justice Scoreboard, a report, and are typed in below with the figure they come from. The charts of countries show the 27 EU countries, with Greece in red and the EU as a whole, where there is a figure for it, in blue.

Rankings of countries are a starting point, not a verdict: an investor in a Greek hotel and an investor in a Greek factory face different costs and different risks.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
eu_codes <- eu_countries$code
eu_name <- c(setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code), EU27_2020 = "EU-27")
# a World Bank indicator for the EU countries, with Eurostat's country codes (EL for Greece)
iso3 <- c(BE = "BEL", BG = "BGR", CZ = "CZE", DK = "DNK", DE = "DEU", EE = "EST", IE = "IRL", EL = "GRC",
          ES = "ESP", FR = "FRA", HR = "HRV", IT = "ITA", CY = "CYP", LV = "LVA", LT = "LTU", LU = "LUX",
          HU = "HUN", MT = "MLT", NL = "NLD", AT = "AUT", PL = "POL", PT = "PRT", RO = "ROU", SI = "SVN",
          SK = "SVK", FI = "FIN", SE = "SWE")
world_bank <- function(indicator, years = "2000:2025") {
  url <- paste0("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/", paste(iso3, collapse = ";"), "/indicator/", indicator,
                "?format=json&per_page=5000&date=", years)
  x <- jsonlite::fromJSON(url)[[2]]
  x <- data.frame(geo = names(iso3)[match(x$countryiso3code, iso3)], time = as.numeric(x$date), values = x$value)
  x[!is.na(x$values), ]
}
# investment: gross fixed capital formation (buildings, machines, equipment, software), % of GDP
investment_all <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(na_item = "P51G", unit = "PC_GDP"))
# foreign direct investment, net inflows, % of GDP
fdi_all <- world_bank("BX.KLT.DINV.WD.GD.ZS")
# yield of 10-year government bonds, % a year
yields_all <- eurostat_values("irt_lt_mcby_a", list(int_rt = "MCBY"))
# government debt, % of GDP
debt_all <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list(na_item = "GD", sector = "S13", unit = "PC_GDP"))
# GDP growth after inflation, %
growth_all <- eurostat_values("tec00115", list(unit = "CLV_PCH_PRE", na_item = "B1GQ"))
# labour cost per hour, euro, in the business economy
labour_all <- eurostat_values("lc_lci_lev", list(lcstruct = "D1_D4_MD5", nace_r2 = "B-S_X_O", unit = "EUR"))
# electricity for businesses using 2 to 20 GWh a year, euro per kWh without VAT, every six months
electricity_all <- eurostat_values("nrg_pc_205", list(nrg_cons = "MWH2000-19999", tax = "X_VAT", currency = "EUR", unit = "KWH"))
# renewable energy, % of the energy used
renewables_all <- eurostat_values("nrg_ind_ren", list(nrg_bal = "REN", unit = "PC"))
# World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators, from about -2.5 (worst) to +2.5 (best)
governance_names <- c(GOV_WGI_GE.EST = "Government effectiveness", GOV_WGI_RQ.EST = "Regulatory quality",
                      GOV_WGI_RL.EST = "Rule of law", GOV_WGI_CC.EST = "Control of corruption")
governance_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(governance_names), function(code) {
  cbind(world_bank(code, "2010:2025"), indicator = governance_names[[code]])
}))
# World Bank Logistics Performance Index, from 1 (worst) to 5 (best)
logistics_all <- world_bank("LP.LPI.OVRL.XQ", "2010:2025")
Code 
# European Commission, The 2026 EU Justice Scoreboard (June 2026), Figure 52: how companies perceive
# the effectiveness of investment protection by the law and courts (Eurobarometer, 2026), % of companies
protection <- data.frame(
  geo = c("SE", "IE", "FI", "LU", "DK", "AT", "NL", "MT", "SI", "CZ", "FR", "HR", "IT", "DE",
          "BE", "LT", "RO", "ES", "HU", "EE", "BG", "LV", "PT", "SK", "CY", "PL", "EL"),
  very_confident     = c(39, 26, 26, 25, 41, 21, 18, 18,  8, 14, 14,  8,  4, 19, 13,  4,  5, 10, 11,  5,  4,  2,  6,  1,  1,  8,  5),
  fairly_confident   = c(49, 55, 55, 54, 37, 53, 53, 50, 59, 50, 47, 49, 53, 37, 43, 52, 48, 42, 38, 42, 43, 43, 37, 34, 34, 24, 20),
  fairly_unconfident = c(10, 13, 15, 10, 10, 11, 18, 11, 20, 18, 23, 28, 33, 27, 27, 31, 34, 29, 35, 36, 35, 38, 40, 43, 35, 42, 34),
  very_unconfident   = c( 0,  3,  3,  3,  9, 13,  7, 10, 12, 14, 15, 13,  9, 10, 14, 10, 12, 17, 12,  9, 13, 14, 11, 18, 29, 22, 36),
  dont_know          = c( 2,  3,  1,  8,  3,  2,  4, 11,  1,  4,  1,  2,  1,  7,  3,  3,  1,  2,  4,  8,  5,  3,  6,  4,  1,  4,  5)
)
protection$time <- 2026
protection$values <- protection$very_confident + protection$fairly_confident
# Figure 5: estimated time needed to resolve litigious civil and commercial cases at first instance,
# 2024, in days (CEPEJ study), read from the chart: Greece, and the next two slowest countries
court_days <- c(EL = 740, CY = 680, IT = 590)
Code 
# the EU countries and the EU in the latest year with data for Greece and for most EU countries
latest <- function(x, at_least = 20) {
  x <- x[x$geo %in% c(eu_codes, "EU27_2020"), ]
  for (y in sort(unique(x$time[x$geo == "EL"]), decreasing = TRUE)) {
    if (sum(x$geo %in% eu_codes & x$time == y) >= at_least) return(x[x$time == y, ])
  }
  stop("No year with data for Greece and for most EU countries")
}
greece <- function(x) x$values[x$geo == "EL"]
median_eu <- function(x) median(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])
# the EU: its own figure where there is one, otherwise the median of the countries
eu <- function(x) if (any(x$geo == "EU27_2020")) x$values[x$geo == "EU27_2020"] else median_eu(x)
countries <- function(x) sum(x$geo %in% eu_codes)
ordinal <- function(k) {
  paste0(k, if (k %% 100 %in% 11:13) "th" else c("th", "st", "nd", "rd", rep("th", 6))[k %% 10 + 1])
}
# the place of Greece among the EU countries, counted from the nearer end: "the highest",
# "the 3rd highest", "the 2nd lowest", ...
place <- function(x) {
  v <- x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes]
  from_top <- sum(v > greece(x)) + 1
  from_bottom <- sum(v < greece(x)) + 1
  k <- min(from_top, from_bottom)
  end <- if (from_top <= from_bottom) "highest" else "lowest"
  paste("the", if (k == 1) end else paste(ordinal(k), end))
}
# one series of a dataset, for Greece or the EU
series <- function(x, geo) x[x$geo == geo, c("time", "values")]
at <- function(x, geo, year) x$values[x$geo == geo & x$time == year]
investment <- latest(investment_all)
fdi <- latest(fdi_all)
yields <- latest(yields_all)
debt <- latest(debt_all)
growth <- latest(growth_all)
labour <- latest(labour_all)
electricity <- latest(electricity_all)
renewables <- latest(renewables_all)
logistics <- latest(logistics_all)
governance <- lapply(split(governance_all, governance_all$indicator), latest)[governance_names]
Code 
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = modifyList(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = modifyList(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the EU countries from the highest to the lowest, Greece in red and the EU in blue; where there is
# no figure for the EU, a dotted line marks the median country
ranking <- function(x, title, source, suffix = "%", digits = 1) {
  x <- x[x$geo %in% c(eu_codes, "EU27_2020"), ]
  x$name <- eu_name[x$geo]
  x <- x[order(x$values), ]
  x$name <- factor(x$name, levels = x$name)
  lines <- list()
  notes <- list()
  if (!any(x$geo == "EU27_2020")) {
    m <- median(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])
    lines <- list(list(type = "line", x0 = m, x1 = m, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper", line = list(color = blue, width = 2, dash = "dot")))
    notes <- list(list(x = m, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "Median EU country", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
                       xshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = blue)))
  }
  # the source 45 px under the plot, below the numbers of the axis
  height <- knitr::opts_current$get("out.height.px")
  if (!is.numeric(height)) height <- 864
  plot_ly(x,
    x = ~values, y = ~name, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = ifelse(x$geo == "EL", greek_red, ifelse(x$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: %{x:.", digits, "f}", suffix, "<extra></extra>")
  ) %>%
    chart(paste0(title, ", ", floor(x$time[1])), source, x_axis = list(ticksuffix = suffix), shapes = lines,
          annotations = notes, margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -45 / (height - 70 - 90))
}
# Greece and a second line (the EU, or another country) over time
two_lines <- function(a, b, name_b, title, source, y_title, suffix = "%", digits = 1, y_axis = list(), ...) {
  plot_ly(a, x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Greece",
    line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.", digits, "f}", suffix, "<extra>Greece</extra>")) %>%
    add_trace(data = b, x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = name_b,
      line = list(color = blue, width = 3), inherit = FALSE,
      hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.", digits, "f}", suffix, "<extra>", name_b, "</extra>")) %>%
    chart(title, source, y_title, y_axis = modifyList(list(ticksuffix = suffix), y_axis), legend = legend_top, ...)
}
# short labels of numbers
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2)

1. Do investors invest in Greece?

Code 
investment_line <- series(investment_all, "EL")
peak_year <- investment_line$time[which.max(investment_line$values)]
low_year <- investment_line$time[which.min(investment_line$values)]

Less than in almost all the EU, though more than at the bottom of the crisis. In 2025, Greece invested 18.0% of its GDP in buildings, machines, equipment and software, against 21.5% in the EU: the 3rd lowest share of the 27 countries. Before the crisis it invested more than the EU, 25.9% of GDP in 2000; by 2019 it had fallen to 11.0%. An economy that invests less than it did, and less than its neighbours, adds little to what it can produce.

Code 
two_lines(investment_line, series(investment_all, "EU27_2020"), "EU-27",
          "Investment, % of GDP", "Eurostat, nama_10_gdp (gross fixed capital formation)", "% of GDP",
          y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"))

Interactive chart: Investment, % of GDP

Code 
fdi_median <- aggregate(values ~ time, fdi_all[fdi_all$geo %in% eu_codes, ], median)
fdi_years <- fdi_median$time[fdi_median$time >= max(fdi_median$time) - 4]
fdi_recent <- mean(at(fdi_all, "EL", fdi_years))
fdi_recent_eu <- mean(fdi_median$values[fdi_median$time %in% fdi_years])
fdi_before <- series(fdi_all, "EL")
fdi_before <- fdi_before[fdi_before$time < min(fdi_years), ]

Foreign investors have come back. Foreign direct investment, money from abroad that buys or builds a lasting share in Greek companies, averaged 3.0% of GDP a year in 2021-2025, against 3.0% in the median EU country; in 2000-2020 it had averaged 1.0%. The chart compares Greece with the median EU country, because the figures of a few countries, such as Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Ireland, swing by tens of percent of GDP with money that only passes through them.

Code 
two_lines(series(fdi_all, "EL"), fdi_median, "Median EU country",
          "Foreign direct investment, net inflows, % of GDP", "World Bank, BX.KLT.DINV.WD.GD.ZS", "% of GDP")

Interactive chart: Foreign direct investment, net inflows, % of GDP

2. Is the country a financial risk?

Code 
# since 2001, when Greece joined the euro: before, its bonds were in drachmas
greek_yields <- series(yields_all[yields_all$time >= 2001, ], "EL")
german_yields <- series(yields_all[yields_all$time >= 2001, ], "DE")
spread <- merge(greek_yields, german_yields, by = "time", suffixes = c("_el", "_de"))
spread$values <- spread$values_el - spread$values_de
worst <- spread[which.max(spread$values), ]
now <- spread[nrow(spread), ]
debt_line <- series(debt_all, "EL")
debt_peak <- debt_line[which.max(debt_line$values), ]

The markets no longer see Greece as a high risk, but its debt is the highest in the EU.

The interest rate that a country pays on its bonds is what the markets think of its risk. In 2012, in the debt crisis, Greece’s 10-year bonds paid 22.5% a year, 21.0 points more than Germany’s. In 2025 they paid 3.4%, only 0.8 points more than Germany’s and no more than the EU average of 3.4%. The credit rating agencies agree. They cut Greece to junk in the crisis, but S&P, Fitch, DBRS and Scope have rated it investment grade again since 2023, and Moody’s since 2025, so the large funds that may hold only such bonds can buy Greek debt again.

Code 
two_lines(greek_yields, german_yields, "Germany",
          "Yield of 10-year government bonds, % a year", "Eurostat, irt_lt_mcby_a", "% a year",
          y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"))

Interactive chart: Yield of 10-year government bonds, % a year

The debt that worried the markets is still there: 145.4% of GDP in 2025, the highest in the EU, where it is 81.5%, though down from 209.4% in 2020. Much of it is owed to other euro countries on long terms and low interest rates, which is why the markets accept it. The economy grew by 2.1% in 2025, against 1.4% in the EU.

Code 
two_lines(debt_line, series(debt_all, "EU27_2020"), "EU-27",
          "Government debt, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "% of GDP",
          y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"))

Interactive chart: Government debt, % of GDP

3. What does it cost to produce there?

Cheap labour, electricity at about the EU’s price.

An hour of work cost employers in Greece €18.2 in 2025, wages and the employers’ contributions together, against €34.9 in the EU: the 6th lowest of 26 countries. Labour is cheap partly because it produces little: an hour of work in Greece produces about half of what it produces on average in the EU (see Greece at Work).

Code 
ranking(labour, "Labour cost per hour, euro", "Eurostat, lc_lci_lev (business economy)", suffix = "", digits = 1)

Interactive chart: Labour cost per hour, euro, 2025

Code 
half <- function(t) paste0(if (t %% 1 == 0) "first" else "second", " half of ", floor(t))
greek_power <- series(electricity_all, "EL")
eu_power <- series(electricity_all, "EU27_2020")
power_peak <- greek_power[which.max(greek_power$values), ]

Electricity matters most for factories, data centres and cold storage. In the first half of 2026, a business that uses 2 to 20 GWh a year, a medium-sized factory, paid 16.0 cents per kWh in Greece before VAT, against 15.6 cents in the EU: the 11th highest of 27 countries. In the energy crisis the price rose to 22.9 cents, in the second half of 2022. Renewables, which keep the price of electricity from following the price of gas, gave 26.9% of the energy used in Greece in 2025, against 26.2% in the EU.

Code 
power <- function(x) transform(x, values = 100 * values)
two_lines(power(greek_power[greek_power$time >= 2015, ]), power(eu_power[eu_power$time >= 2015, ]), "EU-27",
          "Electricity for medium-sized businesses, cents per kWh, without VAT",
          "Eurostat, nrg_pc_205 (2 to 20 GWh a year, every six months)", "Cents per kWh", suffix = "", digits = 1,
          y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"))

Interactive chart: Electricity for medium-sized businesses, cents per kWh, without VAT

4. How well does the state work?

Code 
gov_table <- data.frame(
  indicator = factor(governance_names, levels = rev(governance_names)),
  greece = sapply(governance, greece),
  median = sapply(governance, median_eu),
  low = sapply(governance, function(x) min(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])),
  high = sapply(governance, function(x) max(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])),
  place = sapply(governance, place),
  year = sapply(governance, function(x) x$time[1])
)
g <- function(name, column) gov_table[[column]][gov_table$indicator == name]

Bureaucracy and law and order: in the bottom third of the EU. The World Bank combines surveys of companies, households and experts into four measures of how well the state works: how good the public administration is (government effectiveness), how well regulation lets private business work (regulatory quality), how far contracts, property rights, the police and the courts can be relied on (rule of law), and how little public power is used for private gain (control of corruption). Each runs from about -2.5 to +2.5. In 2025, Greece had the 2nd lowest score of the EU for government effectiveness, the 6th lowest for regulatory quality, the 3rd lowest for the rule of law and the 7th lowest for control of corruption. All four are better than those of most countries in the world, but they are below the EU’s middle.

Code 
plot_ly(gov_table) %>%
  add_segments(x = ~low, xend = ~high, y = ~indicator, yend = ~indicator, name = "EU countries, lowest to highest",
               line = list(color = "#d9d9d9", width = 10), hoverinfo = "skip") %>%
  add_markers(x = ~median, y = ~indicator, name = "Median EU country", marker = list(color = blue, size = 13, symbol = "line-ns-open", line = list(width = 3, color = blue)),
              hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.2f}<extra>Median EU country</extra>") %>%
  add_markers(x = ~greece, y = ~indicator, name = "Greece", marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 13),
              hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.2f}<extra>Greece</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Worldwide Governance Indicators, ", gov_table$year[1], " (-2.5 worst, +2.5 best)"),
        "World Bank, Worldwide Governance Indicators", legend = legend_top, margin = list(l = 170, t = 90, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Worldwide Governance Indicators, 2025 (-2.5 worst, +2.5 best)

5. Do the courts protect investors?

Greek courts are the slowest in the EU, and Greek companies trust them the least.

An investor needs to know that a contract will be enforced. In 2024, a civil or commercial dispute took about 740 days to be resolved at first instance in Greece, more than two years before any appeal: the longest of the EU countries with data. Cyprus and Italy, the next slowest, needed about 680 and 590 days, and most EU countries fewer than 300 (2026 EU Justice Scoreboard, Figure 5, from the CEPEJ study of the Council of Europe).

Code 
protection_eu <- protection[protection$geo %in% eu_codes, ]
unconfident <- function(code) {
  row <- protection[protection$geo == code, ]
  row$fairly_unconfident + row$very_unconfident
}

Companies see it. Asked in 2026 how well the law and the courts protect their investments, 25% of Greek companies said that they were confident, the lowest share in the EU, where it is 56% in the median country; 70% were not confident, and 36% very unconfident, more than in any other country.

Code 
ranking(protection, "Companies confident that the law and courts protect their investments, %",
        "European Commission, 2026 EU Justice Scoreboard, Figure 52 (Eurobarometer)", digits = 0)

Interactive chart: Companies confident that the law and courts protect their investments, %, 2026

6. Can goods move?

Ports, roads and customs: close to the EU’s middle. The World Bank’s Logistics Performance Index scores, from 1 to 5, how well a country’s customs, ports, roads and railways, shipping and tracking work, from a survey of the companies that move goods. In 2022, Greece scored 3.70, against 3.60 in the median EU country: the 10th highest of 27 countries. Its ports, Piraeus first among them, are among the busiest of the Mediterranean.

Code 
ranking(logistics, "Logistics Performance Index (1 worst, 5 best)", "World Bank, LP.LPI.OVRL.XQ", suffix = "", digits = 2)

Interactive chart: Logistics Performance Index (1 worst, 5 best), 2022

So, is Greece a good place to invest?

It depends on what an investor needs, and the data show which needs Greece meets:

  1. Financial risk is low again: the bonds pay about what the EU’s pay, and the rating agencies call them investment grade, though the debt, 145% of GDP, is the EU’s highest.
  2. Costs are low: labour costs €18.2 an hour against €34.9 in the EU, and electricity is at about the EU’s price.
  3. Investors are coming back, but not enough: foreign investment has risen, yet the economy invests 18% of its GDP, the 3rd lowest share in the EU.
  4. The state is the weak point: the public administration, regulation, the rule of law and the control of corruption are all in the bottom part of the EU.
  5. And the courts most of all: about 740 days for a first judgment, the longest in the EU, and 25% of Greek companies confident that the law protects their investments, the lowest share.

For an investor who needs cheap labour and a growing market, and seldom goes to court, Greece has become a reasonable bet. For one whose investment depends on contracts and permits, the slow courts and the bureaucracy are the risk to price in.

Sources

  • Eurostat: nama_10_gdp (investment), irt_lt_mcby_a (government bond yields), gov_10dd_edpt1 (government debt), tec00115 (GDP growth), lc_lci_lev (labour cost), nrg_pc_205 (electricity prices for non-household consumers), nrg_ind_ren (renewable energy).
  • World Bank: foreign direct investment, net inflows, Worldwide Governance Indicators, Logistics Performance Index.
  • European Commission: The 2026 EU Justice Scoreboard, June 2026 (Figure 5, from the CEPEJ study of the Council of Europe, and Figure 52, from the Eurobarometer survey of companies), © European Union, CC BY 4.0.

item.title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
item.description: Greece against the EU on schooling, PISA scores, digital skills, adult learning, jobs, productivity, overqualification and crime, in Eurostat data.
item.content:encoded:
Greece against the EU on schooling, PISA scores, digital skills, adult learning, jobs, productivity, overqualification and crime, in Eurostat data.

What is this?

Are Greeks good workers? How much schooling do they have, do they know maths, can they use a computer, do they find work, and is there much crime? None of these questions has a single number for an answer, but each has measures that every EU country collects in the same way, so Greece can be compared with the rest of the EU:

  1. How much schooling do Greeks have?
  2. What do they know? Maths, reading and science at 15, computer skills, and learning as adults.
  3. Do they find work?
  4. How hard do they work, and how much do they produce?
  5. Do their jobs use their education?
  6. Is there much crime?

The data come from Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU. They are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures. The charts of countries show the 27 EU countries, with Greece in red and the EU as a whole in blue.

What these numbers can and cannot say. They describe what the schools, the firms and the courts of Greece produce, not what Greeks are born with: no statistic measures how intelligent or how hard-working a people is. A test at 15 measures what a school system has taught by then. Output per hour measures the firms, the machines and the way the economy is organised as much as the people who work in it. And recorded crime depends on how often people go to the police, and on how each country counts offences.

# the EU countries and the EU in the latest year with data for Greece and for most EU countries
latest <- function(x) {
  x <- x[x$geo %in% c(eu_codes, "EU27_2020"), ]
  for (y in sort(unique(x$time[x$geo == "EL"]), decreasing = TRUE)) {
    if (sum(x$geo %in% eu_codes & x$time == y) >= 20) return(x[x$time == y, ])
  }
  stop("No year with data for Greece and for most EU countries")
}

ordinal <- function(k) {
  paste0(k, if (k %% 100 %in% 11:13) "th" else c("th", "st", "nd", "rd", rep("th", 6))[k %% 10 + 1])

# the place of Greece among the EU countries, counted from the nearer end: "the highest",
# "the 3rd highest", "the 2nd lowest", ...
place <- function(x) {
  v <- x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes]
  from_top <- sum(v > greece(x)) + 1
  from_bottom <- sum(v < greece(x)) + 1
  k <- min(from_top, from_bottom)
  end <- if (from_top <= from_bottom) "highest" else "lowest"
  paste("the", if (k == 1) end else paste(ordinal(k), end))
}

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = modifyList(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = modifyList(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the EU countries from the highest to the lowest, Greece in red and the EU in blue; where Eurostat
# publishes no figure for the EU, a dotted line marks the median country
ranking <- function(x, title, source, suffix = "%", digits = 1) {
  x$name <- eu_name[x$geo]
  x <- x[order(x$values), ]
  x$name <- factor(x$name, levels = x$name)
  lines <- list()
  notes <- list()
  if (!any(x$geo == "EU27_2020")) {
    m <- median(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])
    lines <- list(list(type = "line", x0 = m, x1 = m, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper", line = list(color = blue, width = 2, dash = "dot")))
    notes <- list(list(x = m, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "Median EU country", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
                       xshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = blue)))
  }
  # the source 45 px under the plot, below the numbers of the axis: in a chart this tall a fixed
  # fraction of the plot would put it below the bottom of the chart
  height <- knitr::opts_current$get("out.height.px")
  if (!is.numeric(height)) height <- 864
  plot_ly(x,
    x = ~values, y = ~name, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = ifelse(x$geo == "EL", greek_red, ifelse(x$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: %{x:.", digits, "f}", suffix, "<extra></extra>")
  ) %>%
    chart(paste0(title, ", ", x$time[1]), source, x_axis = list(ticksuffix = suffix), shapes = lines,
          annotations = notes, margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -45 / (height - 70 - 90))
}

1. How much schooling do Greeks have?

About as many university graduates as the rest of the EU, and almost no one leaves school early.

In 2025, 42.8% of Greeks aged 25 to 34 had a university degree or another tertiary qualification, against 44.8% in the EU: the 11th lowest share of the 27 countries.

Almost every young Greek finishes secondary school. Only 3.0% of Greeks aged 18 to 24 left education with at most lower secondary school and are not in any education or training, the 2nd lowest share in the EU, where it is 9.1%. The older generations had less schooling: 18.0% of Greeks aged 25 to 64 have no more than lower secondary education, against 18.8% in the EU.

2. What do they know?

Maths, reading and science at 15

Code 
pisa_year <- pisa$EF461$time[1]
maths <- pisa_all[pisa_all$field == "EF461" & pisa_all$geo %in% c("EL", "EU27_2020"), ]
first_year <- min(intersect(maths$time[maths$geo == "EL"], maths$time[maths$geo == "EU27_2020"]))
maths_then <- function(geo) maths$values[maths$geo == geo & maths$time == first_year]

50% of Greek 15-year-olds are below the basic level in maths, against 34% in the EU.

PISA, the OECD’s test of 15-year-olds, measures whether students can use what they have learned. Below level 2, its basic level, a student can at most answer questions about a familiar, clearly stated situation with all the information given: in maths, for example, apply a simple formula when told which one. In 2025, 50% of Greek 15-year-olds were below that level in maths, against 34% in the EU, the 4th highest share of the 27 countries. In reading the shares are 44% and 31%, and in science 41% and 26%. The EU’s target for 2030 is fewer than 15% in each.

Computer skills

51% of Greek adults have at least basic computer skills, against 60% in the EU.

Eurostat counts people as having at least basic digital skills when they can do at least one basic task in each of five areas: finding and judging information, communicating online, making digital content, using a device safely, and solving problems with it. In 2025, 51% of Greeks aged 16 to 74 could, against 60% in the EU, the 6th lowest share of the 27 countries; 27% had above basic skills, against 31%. Few Greeks work with computers for a living: ICT specialists are 2.5% of the people in work, the lowest share in the EU, where they are 5.0%.

Code

Unemployment in Greece lasts: 56% of the unemployed have been looking for work for a year or longer, against 32% in the EU, which makes the long-term unemployed 5.0% of the labour force, the highest share in the EU. 13.6% of Greeks aged 15 to 29 are neither in work nor in education or training, against 11.0% in the EU.

Of the Greeks aged 20 to 64, 71.0% have a job, against 76.1% in the EU. The gap is mostly among women: 62.3% of Greek women have a job, against 71.3% of women in the EU, while for men the rates are 79.7% and 80.9%.

4. How hard do they work, and how much do they produce?

Hours of work: the highest in the EU. Output per hour: the lowest.

Greeks in work usually work 41.0 hours a week, the highest in the EU, where the average is 37.0. Yet an hour of work in Greece produces 54% of what an hour produces on average in the EU, the lowest in the EU, and a person in work, with the longer hours, 67%. These figures count output in purchasing power standards, which allow for the lower prices of Greece.

Output per hour depends less on how hard people work than on what they work with, and where. A large share of Greeks work for themselves or in very small firms: 24.3% of Greeks in work are self-employed, the highest share in the EU, where it is 12.9%. They run farms, shops, taxis, cafés and workshops, often with no employees. Small businesses like these have less machinery and technology behind each hour of work than large firms, and long opening hours add hours more than they add output.

Often not. 31.4% of the Greeks with tertiary education who work have jobs that do not need it, such as clerical, sales or manual jobs, the 2nd highest share in the EU, where it is 21.4%. The schools and universities produce graduates; the economy has too few jobs that need them.

6. Is there much crime?

Recorded crime is around the middle of the EU, but the share of Greeks who see crime around them is the highest in the EU.

Crime is hard to compare between countries. The police can only count the offences that people report, and people report more where they trust the police or need a report for their insurance; and each country defines and counts offences in its own way. Eurostat therefore warns against comparing the levels of most offences between countries. The exception is intentional homicide, which is almost always recorded, and recorded in the same way.

How many are in prison?

Code 
prison_year <- max(prisoners_ctz$time)
held <- function(citizen) prisoners_ctz$values[prisoners_ctz$citizen == citizen & prisoners_ctz$time == prison_year]
# the Greek citizens living in Greece on 1 January of the next year, or of the same year
greek_citizens <- citizens$values[match(prison_year + 1, citizens$time)]
if (is.na(greek_citizens)) greek_citizens <- citizens$values[match(prison_year, citizens$time)]
greek_rate <- 1e5 * held("NAT") / greek_citizens

Greece holds 111 people in prison for every 100,000 inhabitants, against 111 in the median EU country (the 14th highest rate of 27). Of the 11,484 people held in Greek prisons in 2024, 5,511 were Greek citizens: 57 for every 100,000 Greek citizens living in Greece, or one in 1,748. The other 52% were foreign citizens, a group that also includes people who did not live in Greece, so it cannot be turned into a rate in the same way.

A prison count is not a count of criminals: it includes people waiting for their trial, and most people who commit an offence are never caught, or are fined or given a suspended sentence instead of prison.

How safe do Greeks feel?

Less safe than anyone else in the EU. In 2023, 20.9% of Greeks said that there is crime, violence or vandalism in the area where they live, against 10.0% of people in the EU: the highest share. The gap between the crime that is recorded and the crime that people see around them can have many causes, among them petty crime and vandalism that are never reported, and trust in the police.

Code 
ranking(area, "People who say that their area has crime, violence or vandalism, %", "Eurostat, ilc_mddw03 (EU-SILC)")

Interactive chart: People who say that their area has crime, violence or vandalism, %, 2023

So, are they good workers?

The data cannot say whether Greeks are good workers, but they can say what Greek workers bring and what the economy does with it:

  1. They work long hours: 41.0 hours a week, the highest in the EU.
  2. They stay in education: the 2nd lowest share of early school leavers in the EU, and about as many graduates as the EU, 43% of people aged 25 to 34.
  3. But what they learn at school is weak: 50% of 15-year-olds are below the basic level in maths, against 34% in the EU; fewer adults have basic computer skills (51%, against 60%), and almost none go back to learning (5.2%, the lowest share in the EU).
  4. And the economy does not use what they have: an hour of work produces 54% of the EU average, the lowest; 24% of the people in work are self-employed, mostly in very small businesses; 31% of the graduates in work have jobs that do not need a degree; and 9% of the labour force cannot find work.
  5. Crime is not the problem it is felt to be: the homicide rate and the prison population are around the middle of the EU, and 57 in every 100,000 Greek citizens are in prison, yet 21% of Greeks say that there is crime where they live, the highest share in the EU.

The picture is of people who work hard and stay in school, in an economy of small businesses that turns their hours into little output and leaves much of their education unused, and with schools that teach less than those of most of the EU.

Sources

  • Eurostat, education and skills: edat_lfse_03 (educational attainment), edat_lfse_14 (early leavers from education and training), sdg_04_40 (low achieving 15-year-olds, from the OECD’s PISA), isoc_sk_dskl_i21 (digital skills), trng_lfse_01 (adult learning), isoc_sks_itspt (ICT specialists).
  • Eurostat, work: une_rt_a (unemployment), une_ltu_a (long-term unemployment), edat_lfse_20 (young people neither in employment nor in education or training), lfsi_emp_a (employment), lfsa_ewhun2 (hours of work), tesem160 (labour productivity), lfsa_egaps (employment by professional status), lfsa_eoqgan (over-qualification).
  • Eurostat, crime: crim_off_cat (recorded offences), crim_pris_cap (prison population), crim_pris_ctz (prisoners by citizenship), migr_pop1ctz (population by citizenship), ilc_mddw03 (crime, violence or vandalism in the area).

item.title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
item.description: What Greece produces, exports and imports, who its trading partners are and whether it can feed itself, charted in R with Eurostat and FAO data.
item.content:encoded:
What Greece produces, exports and imports, who its trading partners are and whether it can feed itself, charted in R with Eurostat and FAO data.

What is this?

What does the Greek economy live on? This story follows the money through the economy and across its borders, and the food through its farms, seas and ports:

  1. What does Greece produce?
  2. Who buys it?
  3. How much does Greece sell abroad, and how much does it buy?
  4. What does it sell and buy, and with whom?
  5. Can Greece feed itself?

The data come from three places:

  • Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU: the national accounts, which split the economy into what each industry produces and into who spends the money, and the balance of payments, which records what Greece sells and buys abroad in services, such as tourism and shipping.
  • Comext, Eurostat’s database of trade in goods, which records every good that crosses the borders of an EU country: what it is, where it comes from or goes to, and what it is worth.
  • FAOSTAT, the statistics of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, whose food balance sheets weigh, for each food, what a country produces, imports, exports and eats.

They are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite", "countrycode"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
# the industries of the national accounts (NACE); energy, water and mining are all industry (B-E)
# without manufacturing (C)
industries <- c(
  A = "Agriculture, forestry and fishing", BE_C = "Energy, water and mining", C = "Manufacturing",
  F = "Construction", "G-I" = "Trade, transport, hotels and restaurants", J = "Information and communication",
  K = "Finance and insurance", L = "Real estate", M_N = "Professional and business services",
  "O-Q" = "Public administration, education and health", "R-U" = "Arts, leisure and other services"
)
# what each industry produces (gross value added, million euros) and the people who work in it (thousands)
gva <- eurostat_values("nama_10_a10", list(geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), unit = "CP_MEUR", na_item = "B1G"))
jobs <- eurostat_values("nama_10_a10_e", list(geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), unit = "THS_PER", na_item = "EMP_DC"))
# the share of each industry in the total, %
shares <- function(x, geo, year) {
  x <- x[x$geo == geo & x$time == year, ]
  v <- setNames(x$values, x$nace_r2)
  v["BE_C"] <- v["B-E"] - v["C"]
  100 * v[names(industries)] / v["TOTAL"]
}
gva_year <- max(gva$time[gva$geo == "EL"])
job_year <- max(jobs$time[jobs$geo == "EL"])
# GDP by who spends it, % of GDP and million euros: households (with the non-profit institutions that
# serve them), government, investment (gross capital formation), exports and imports, of goods and of services
uses <- c(P31_S14_S15 = "Households", P3_S13 = "Government", P5G = "Investment", P6 = "Exports", P7 = "Imports")
accounts <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(
  geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), unit = c("PC_GDP", "CP_MEUR"), na_item = c(names(uses), "P61", "P62", "P71", "P72")
))
gdp_year <- max(accounts$time[accounts$geo == "EL"])
account <- function(item, geo = "EL", year = gdp_year, unit = "PC_GDP") {
  accounts$values[accounts$na_item == item & accounts$geo == geo & accounts$time == year & accounts$unit == unit]
}
# services sold to (CRE) and bought from (DEB) the rest of the world, million euros: all services (S),
# travel (SD), transport (SC), sea transport (SC1) and its freight (SC12)
services <- eurostat_values("bop_its6_det", list(
  geo = "EL", partner = "WRL_REST", currency = "MIO_EUR", stk_flow = c("CRE", "DEB"), bop_item = c("S", "SD", "SC", "SC1", "SC12")
))
service <- function(item, flow = "CRE", year) services$values[services$bop_item == item & services$stk_flow == flow & services$time == year]
services_year <- max(services$time[services$bop_item == "S"])
sea_year <- max(services$time[services$bop_item == "SC1"])
# Comext, Eurostat's database of trade in goods, from its own API (the eurostat package does not
# read it): a JSON-stat dataset, its values in one vector in the order of its dimensions, the last
# changing fastest
comext <- function(filters, id = "DS-045409") {
  query <- paste(paste0(rep(names(filters), lengths(filters)), "=", unlist(filters)), collapse = "&")
  x <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0("https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/comext/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/", id, "?", query))
  codes <- lapply(x$id, function(d) names(sort(unlist(x$dimension[[d]]$category$index))))
  grid <- expand.grid(rev(codes), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)   # the first dimension changes fastest
  names(grid) <- rev(x$id)
  grid$values <- NA
  grid$values[as.integer(names(x$value)) + 1] <- unlist(x$value)
  grid <- grid[!is.na(grid$values), ]
  grid$time <- as.integer(grid$time)
  grid
}
# Greece's exports (flow 2) and imports (flow 1) of goods each year since 2019, in euros; with no
# partner, with each partner
trade <- function(product, partner = NULL) {
  comext(list(reporter = "GR", partner = partner, product = product, flow = c("1", "2"),
    indicators = "VALUE_IN_EUROS", freq = "A", sinceTimePeriod = "2019"))
}
# the chapters of the Harmonized System, the classification of goods in trade, by short names
chapters <- c(
  "01" = "Live animals", "02" = "Meat", "03" = "Fish and seafood", "04" = "Dairy, eggs and honey",
  "05" = "Other animal products", "06" = "Plants and flowers", "07" = "Vegetables", "08" = "Fruit and nuts",
  "09" = "Coffee, tea and spices", "10" = "Cereals", "11" = "Flour", "12" = "Oil seeds", "13" = "Gums and resins",
  "14" = "Other plant materials", "15" = "Olive oil and other fats", "16" = "Prepared meat and fish",
  "17" = "Sugar and sweets", "18" = "Cocoa and chocolate", "19" = "Bread, pasta and pastry",
  "20" = "Preserved fruit and vegetables", "21" = "Other food preparations", "22" = "Drinks",
  "23" = "Animal feed", "24" = "Tobacco", "25" = "Salt, stone and cement", "26" = "Ores",
  "27" = "Fuels and oil products", "28" = "Inorganic chemicals", "29" = "Organic chemicals", "30" = "Medicines",
  "31" = "Fertilisers", "32" = "Paints and dyes", "33" = "Cosmetics", "34" = "Soaps and detergents",
  "35" = "Glues and enzymes", "36" = "Explosives", "37" = "Photographic goods", "38" = "Other chemicals",
  "39" = "Plastics", "40" = "Rubber", "41" = "Hides and leather", "42" = "Leather goods", "43" = "Furs",
  "44" = "Wood", "45" = "Cork", "46" = "Basketwork", "47" = "Pulp", "48" = "Paper", "49" = "Printed matter",
  "50" = "Silk", "51" = "Wool", "52" = "Cotton", "53" = "Other plant fibres", "54" = "Man-made filaments",
  "55" = "Man-made fibres", "56" = "Wadding and ropes", "57" = "Carpets", "58" = "Special fabrics",
  "59" = "Coated fabrics", "60" = "Knitted fabrics", "61" = "Knitted clothes", "62" = "Other clothes",
  "63" = "Other textile articles", "64" = "Footwear", "65" = "Headwear", "66" = "Umbrellas",
  "67" = "Feathers and artificial flowers", "68" = "Stone articles", "69" = "Ceramics", "70" = "Glass",
  "71" = "Jewellery and gold", "72" = "Iron and steel", "73" = "Iron and steel articles", "74" = "Copper",
  "75" = "Nickel", "76" = "Aluminium", "78" = "Lead", "79" = "Zinc", "80" = "Tin", "81" = "Other base metals",
  "82" = "Tools", "83" = "Other metal articles", "84" = "Machinery", "85" = "Electrical equipment",
  "86" = "Railway equipment", "87" = "Cars and other vehicles", "88" = "Aircraft", "89" = "Ships and boats",
  "90" = "Instruments", "91" = "Clocks and watches", "92" = "Musical instruments", "93" = "Arms",
  "94" = "Furniture", "95" = "Toys and sports goods", "96" = "Other manufactured articles",
  "97" = "Art and antiques", "99" = "Other goods"
)
goods <- trade(names(chapters), "WORLD")
trade_year <- max(goods$time)
# exports and imports of each chapter in a year, million euros
by_chapter <- function(codes, year = trade_year) {
  x <- data.frame(code = codes, name = unname(chapters[codes]))
  x$exports <- sapply(codes, function(k) sum(goods$values[goods$product == k & goods$flow == "2" & goods$time == year])) / 1e6
  x$imports <- sapply(codes, function(k) sum(goods$values[goods$product == k & goods$flow == "1" & goods$time == year])) / 1e6
  x
}
# crude oil (2709), oil products (2710) and gas (2711)
oil <- trade(c("2709", "2710", "2711"), "WORLD")
oil_trade <- function(code, flow, year = trade_year) sum(oil$values[oil$product == code & oil$flow == flow & oil$time == year]) / 1e6
# the trading partners: countries only, with their names (Comext calls Serbia XS)
partners <- trade("TOTAL")
partners <- partners[partners$time == trade_year, ]
partners$name <- countrycode::countrycode(partners$partner, "iso2c", "country.name", warn = FALSE,
  custom_match = c(TR = "Türkiye", XS = "Serbia", XK = "Kosovo"))
partners <- partners[!is.na(partners$name), ]
# FAOSTAT's food balance sheets for the countries of Europe, from its bulk download, Greece only;
# quantities in thousand tonnes, and the calories of the food each person eats a day
fao_zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file("https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_Europe.zip", fao_zip, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
fbs <- read.csv(unz(fao_zip, "FoodBalanceSheets_E_Europe_NOFLAG.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
fbs <- fbs[fbs$Area == "Greece", ]
fao_years <- as.integer(sub("^Y", "", grep("^Y[0-9]{4}$", names(fbs), value = TRUE)))
fao_year <- max(fao_years[sapply(fao_years, function(y) any(!is.na(fbs[fbs$Element == "Production", paste0("Y", y)])))])
balance <- function(code, element, year = fao_year) {
  v <- fbs[fbs$`Item Code` == code & fbs$Element == element, paste0("Y", year)]
  if (length(v) && !is.na(v[1])) v[1] else NA
}
# what Greece produces of a food, % of what it uses (production / domestic supply): its self-sufficiency
self_sufficiency <- function(code, year = fao_year) {
  produced <- balance(code, "Production", year)
  100 * (if (is.na(produced)) 0 else produced) / balance(code, "Domestic supply quantity", year)
}
eu_name <- c(EL = "Greece", EU27_2020 = "EU-27")
Code 
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels
amber <- "#c97b1e"       # told apart from blue also with colour blindness
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    # at the top, so that a legend of two or three rows fits under it in a larger top margin
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# horizontal bars of two series side by side for each label, the labels from the top in their order
paired_bars <- function(labels, first, second, names, colors, hover) {
  y <- factor(labels, levels = rev(labels))
  plot_ly() %>%
    # plotly draws the first series at the bottom of each pair, so the second goes in first
    add_trace(y = y, x = second, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = names[2], marker = list(color = colors[2]),
      hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: ", hover, "<extra>", names[2], "</extra>")) %>%
    add_trace(y = y, x = first, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = names[1], marker = list(color = colors[1]),
      hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: ", hover, "<extra>", names[1], "</extra>"))
}
# short labels of numbers
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
billion <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE), " billion")   # from million euros
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
# a country's name in a sentence: "the United States"
in_text <- function(name) ifelse(name %in% c("United Kingdom", "United States", "Netherlands"), paste("the", name), name)
# "A", "A and B", "A, B and C"
and_list <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2) x else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])

1. What does Greece produce?

Code 
greece <- shares(gva, "EL", gva_year)
eu <- shares(gva, "EU27_2020", gva_year)
greek_jobs <- shares(jobs, "EL", job_year)
eu_jobs <- shares(jobs, "EU27_2020", job_year)
# the industries with a larger share in Greece than in the EU, the largest difference first
larger <- names(sort((greece - eu)[greece > eu], decreasing = TRUE))
smaller <- names(sort((greece - eu)[greece < eu]))

Mostly services, and above all the ones that serve tourists. Of everything the Greek economy produced in 2025, 26% came from trade, transport, hotels and restaurants, against 19% in the EU. The industries with a larger share in Greece than in the EU are, above all, trade, transport, hotels and restaurants (25.5% against 18.6%), real estate (15.2% against 10.9%) and agriculture, forestry and fishing (4.1% against 1.8%); those with a smaller share, above all, professional and business services (7.2% against 11.9%), manufacturing (11.2% against 15.8%) and construction (2.6% against 5.6%).

Code 
order <- names(sort(greece, decreasing = TRUE))
paired_bars(industries[order], greece[order], eu[order], c("Greece", "EU-27"), c(greek_red, blue), "%{x:.1f}% of the economy") %>%
  chart(paste0("What each industry produces, ", gva_year, ", % of the economy"), "Eurostat, nama_10_a10 (gross value added)",
    barmode = "group", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "reversed"), margin = list(l = 290, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.1)

Interactive chart: What each industry produces, 2025, % of the economy

Three things stand out:

  • Real estate is 15% of the Greek economy. Most of it is not buying and selling houses: the national accounts count the rent that the people who own their homes would pay if they rented them, and most Greeks own their homes.
  • Construction has never recovered from the crisis: 7.8% of the economy in 2007, 2.6% in 2025.
  • Agriculture produces 4.1% of the economy but employs 9.3% of the people who work, against 3.8% in the EU: many small farms, each producing little. Trade, transport, hotels and restaurants employ 37% of the people who work.

2. Who buys it?

Code 
use_shares <- data.frame(item = names(uses), name = uses)
use_shares$greece <- sapply(names(uses), account)
use_shares$eu <- sapply(names(uses), account, geo = "EU27_2020")

Households. GDP is also what is spent on what the economy produces: by households, by the government, on investment, and by foreigners, as exports; and as part of what is spent is produced abroad, imports are taken off. In Greece, households spend 69% of GDP, against 53% in the EU, while investment, in buildings, machines and software, is 17% of GDP, against 22%. Greece consumes a larger share of what it produces, and invests a smaller share, than the EU, and it buys more from abroad than it sells: imports of 44% of GDP, exports of 39%.

Code 
x <- factor(use_shares$name, levels = use_shares$name)
plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(x = x, y = use_shares$greece, type = "bar", name = "Greece", marker = list(color = greek_red),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Greece</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(x = x, y = use_shares$eu, type = "bar", name = "EU-27", marker = list(color = blue),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>EU-27</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Who spends the money: GDP by use, ", gdp_year, ", % of GDP"), "Eurostat, nama_10_gdp", "% of GDP",
  barmode = "group", legend = legend_top,
  annotations = list(list(x = "Imports", y = max(use_shares$greece[5], use_shares$eu[5]), text = "taken off", yanchor = "bottom",
    yshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))))

Interactive chart: Who spends the money: GDP by use, 2025, % of GDP

3. How much does Greece sell abroad, and how much does it buy?

Code 
exports <- accounts[accounts$geo == "EL" & accounts$na_item == "P6" & accounts$unit == "PC_GDP", c("time", "values")]
imports <- accounts[accounts$geo == "EL" & accounts$na_item == "P7" & accounts$unit == "PC_GDP", c("time", "values")]
first <- max(min(exports$time), 1995)
gap <- imports$values[match(exports$time, imports$time)] - exports$values   # % of GDP
surplus_years <- exports$time[exports$time >= first & gap < 0]
widest <- exports$time[exports$time >= first][which.max(gap[exports$time >= first])]
gap_in <- function(year) gap[exports$time == year]

Twice as open as in the 1990s. Greece’s exports of goods and services were 14% of GDP in 1995 and 39% in 2025; its imports, 22% and 44%. In every year since 1995 Greece has bought more from abroad than it sold. The gap was widest in 2008, 11.5 points of GDP, when Greece borrowed abroad to pay for its imports; in 2013, in the crisis, it was 2.3 points, as Greeks could afford much less.

Code 
plot_ly(exports[exports$time >= first, ],
  x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Exports",
  line = list(color = blue, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Exports</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = imports[imports$time >= first, ], x = ~time, y = ~values, name = "Imports",
    line = list(color = amber, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Imports</extra>",
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart("Exports and imports of goods and services, % of GDP", "Eurostat, nama_10_gdp", "% of GDP",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: Exports and imports of goods and services, % of GDP

Code 
goods_gap <- account("P71", unit = "CP_MEUR") - account("P61", unit = "CP_MEUR")
services_gap <- account("P62", unit = "CP_MEUR") - account("P72", unit = "CP_MEUR")

Greece sells services and buys goods. In 2025, it bought €34.1 billion more goods abroad than it sold, and sold €22.5 billion more services than it bought. Two services earn almost all of it:

  • Tourism: in 2025, visitors from abroad spent €23.6 billion in Greece (see the story of Greek tourism).
  • Shipping: Greek shipowners have one of the largest merchant fleets of the world, and the freight their ships earn carrying goods between other countries counts as a Greek export. Sea transport brought in €18.3 billion in 2024, €16.9 billion of it freight.

Together, travel and transport were 83% of the services Greece sold in 2025.

Code 
kinds <- c(Goods = "P61", Services = "P62")
bought <- c(Goods = "P71", Services = "P72")
plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(x = names(kinds), y = sapply(kinds, account, unit = "CP_MEUR") / 1000, type = "bar", name = "Exports",
    marker = list(color = blue), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion<extra>Exports</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(x = names(bought), y = sapply(bought, account, unit = "CP_MEUR") / 1000, type = "bar", name = "Imports",
    marker = list(color = amber), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion<extra>Imports</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Exports and imports of Greece, ", gdp_year, ", € billion"), "Eurostat, nama_10_gdp", "€ billion",
    barmode = "group", legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: Exports and imports of Greece, 2025, € billion

4. What does it sell and buy, and with whom?

Code 
products <- by_chapter(names(chapters))
products$total <- products$exports + products$imports
top_products <- head(products[order(-products$total), ], 14)
top_exports <- head(products[order(-products$exports), ], 5)
fuel_share <- function(flow) 100 * products[[flow]][products$code == "27"] / sum(products[[flow]])

Oil, in both directions. In 2025, Greece exported €48.7 billion of goods and imported €82.5 billion. The largest exports were fuels and oil products (€12.7 billion), aluminium (€2.9 billion), medicines (€2.8 billion), electrical equipment (€2.4 billion) and machinery (€1.8 billion). Fuels are 26% of what Greece sells and 20% of what it buys, because its refineries import crude oil and export what they make of it: Greece bought €8.5 billion of crude oil and sold €10.4 billion of oil products, such as diesel, petrol and fuel for ships and aircraft. It also bought €3.3 billion of natural gas.

Of the rest, Greece imports far more machinery, electrical equipment and cars than it exports, and sells aluminium, medicines and food: fruit, preserved fruit and vegetables, cheese, fish and olive oil.

Code 
paired_bars(top_products$name, top_products$exports / 1000, top_products$imports / 1000, c("Exports", "Imports"), c(blue, amber), "€%{x:.2f} billion") %>%
  chart(paste0("The goods Greece trades most, ", trade_year, ", € billion"), "Eurostat, Comext DS-045409 (chapters of the Harmonized System)",
    barmode = "group", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "reversed"), margin = list(l = 190, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.12)

Interactive chart: The goods Greece trades most, 2025, € billion

Code 
by_partner <- data.frame(code = unique(partners$partner))
by_partner$name <- partners$name[match(by_partner$code, partners$partner)]
by_partner$exports <- sapply(by_partner$code, function(k) sum(partners$values[partners$partner == k & partners$flow == "2"])) / 1e6
by_partner$imports <- sapply(by_partner$code, function(k) sum(partners$values[partners$partner == k & partners$flow == "1"])) / 1e6
top_partners <- head(by_partner[order(-(by_partner$exports + by_partner$imports)), ], 12)
buyers <- head(by_partner[order(-by_partner$exports), ], 5)
sellers <- head(by_partner[order(-by_partner$imports), ], 5)
in_eu <- by_partner$code %in% eu_countries$code
eu_share <- function(flow) 100 * sum(by_partner[[flow]][in_eu]) / sum(by_partner[[flow]])
# countries outside the EU that sell Greece more than €1 billion a year and buy less than a quarter of that
one_way <- by_partner$name[!in_eu & by_partner$imports > 1000 & by_partner$exports < by_partner$imports / 4]

Mostly with its neighbours in the EU. 57% of the goods Greece sells go to the EU, and 55% of those it buys come from it. Its largest customers in 2025 were Italy, Germany, Cyprus, Bulgaria and the United States; its largest suppliers Germany, Italy, China, the Netherlands and France. Azerbaijan, China, India, Iraq, Kazakhstan and Russia sold Greece more than four times as much as they bought from it, mostly oil, gas or manufactured goods.

Code 
paired_bars(top_partners$name, top_partners$exports / 1000, top_partners$imports / 1000, c("Exports to", "Imports from"), c(blue, amber), "€%{x:.2f} billion") %>%
  chart(paste0("Greece's largest trading partners in goods, ", trade_year, ", € billion"), "Eurostat, Comext DS-045409",
    barmode = "group", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "reversed"), margin = list(l = 150, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.12)

Interactive chart: Greece's largest trading partners in goods, 2025, € billion

5. Can Greece feed itself?

Code 
food <- by_chapter(names(chapters)[1:24])
food$balance <- food$exports - food$imports
food_then <- by_chapter(names(chapters)[1:24], 2019)

In money, Greece sells about as much food as it buys. In 2025, it exported €11.8 billion of food, drinks and tobacco and imported €12.7 billion, against €6.1 billion and €7.4 billion in 2019. But it sells and buys different foods. It sells more than it buys of preserved fruit and vegetables, fruit and nuts, olive oil and other fats, tobacco and fish and seafood; it buys far more than it sells of meat, animal feed, coffee, tea and spices, cocoa and chocolate and oil seeds. Meat alone costs it €1.8 billion more than it earns from it.

Code 
shown <- food[abs(food$balance) >= 50, ]
shown <- shown[order(shown$balance), ]
plot_ly(
  y = factor(shown$name, levels = shown$name), x = shown$balance / 1000, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(shown$balance > 0, blue, amber)),
  hovertext = paste0(shown$name, ": exports ", billion(shown$exports), ", imports ", billion(shown$imports)),
  hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Food trade of Greece, exports minus imports, ", trade_year, ", € billion"),
    "Eurostat, Comext DS-045409 (chapters 1 to 24 of the Harmonized System; those under €50 million left out)",
    margin = list(l = 210, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.1,
    annotations = list(
      # above the bars, on each side of zero
      list(x = 0, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "Greece sells more →", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom", xshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = blue)),
      list(x = 0, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "← Greece buys more", xanchor = "right", yanchor = "bottom", xshift = -4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = amber))
    ))

Interactive chart: Food trade of Greece, exports minus imports, 2025, € billion

Money does not tell how much of its food Greece grows. The food balance sheets of FAOSTAT do: for each food, they weigh what Greece produces against what it uses, for food, for animal feed and in factories. A food of which Greece produces more than 100% of what it uses is one it could do without importing; one far below 100% is one it depends on others for.

Code 
foods <- c(
  "2580" = "Olive oil", "2919" = "Fruit", "2918" = "Vegetables", "2732" = "Lamb and goat", "2948" = "Milk",
  "2734" = "Poultry", "2949" = "Eggs", "2911" = "Pulses", "2511" = "Wheat", "2514" = "Maize", "2905" = "All cereals",
  "2943" = "All meat", "2907" = "Potatoes and other roots", "2960" = "Fish and seafood", "2733" = "Pork",
  "2731" = "Beef", "2909" = "Sugar and sweeteners", "2555" = "Soybeans"
)
fed <- data.frame(code = names(foods), name = foods)
fed$ratio <- sapply(fed$code, self_sufficiency)
ratio <- function(code) fed$ratio[fed$code == code]
# the calories of the diet, by the groups that together make up all of it, and the part of each that
# Greek production could cover if all of it stayed in Greece (up to what Greeks eat of it)
diet <- c("2905", "2907", "2908", "2909", "2911", "2912", "2913", "2914", "2918", "2919", "2922", "2923", "2924",
          "2943", "2945", "2946", "2948", "2949", "2960", "2961", "2928")
calories <- data.frame(code = diet, kcal = sapply(diet, balance, element = "Food supply (kcal/capita/day)"))
calories$ratio <- sapply(diet, self_sufficiency)
calories <- calories[!is.na(calories$kcal), ]
calories$covered <- calories$kcal * ifelse(is.na(calories$ratio), 0, pmin(calories$ratio, 100)) / 100
kcal_total <- sum(calories$kcal)
covered <- 100 * sum(calories$covered) / kcal_total
short <- calories$ratio < 70 | is.na(calories$ratio)

Plenty of olive oil, fruit and vegetables; not enough bread, meat or sugar. In 2023, Greece produced 351% of the olive oil it used, 163% of its fruit, 118% of its vegetables and 100% of its lamb and goat meat. But it produced only 66% of its cereals, 54% of its meat (25% of its pork and 24% of its beef), 29% of its fish and seafood and 10% of its sugar. It grows no soybeans, the protein of the feed of pigs and chickens.

Code 
fed <- fed[order(fed$ratio), ]
plot_ly(
  y = factor(fed$name, levels = fed$name), x = fed$ratio, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(fed$ratio >= 100, blue, amber)),
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: Greece produces %{x:.0f}% of what it uses<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("What Greece produces, % of what it uses, ", fao_year), "FAOSTAT, food balance sheets (production / domestic supply)",
    margin = list(l = 180, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.12,
    shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = 100, x1 = 100, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper", line = list(color = dark_gray, dash = "dash"))),
    # at the bottom, next to the shortest bars
    annotations = list(list(x = 100, y = 0, yref = "paper", text = "100%: as much as it uses", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
      xshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))))

Interactive chart: What Greece produces, % of what it uses, 2023

Milk is the least certain of these figures. FAOSTAT counts cheese and yoghurt by the milk it takes to make them, and as Greece’s sales of feta and yoghurt abroad have grown, its milk has risen, on paper, from 56% of what it uses in 2010 to 121% in 2023, while its farms produced 97% of the milk they produced in 2010.

So, would Greece go hungry without imports? No, but it would eat differently. Greece has about 3,380 calories of food a day for each person who lives there: food available, not all of it eaten. If all the food that Greece produces stayed in Greece, it could cover about 70% of these calories, more than enough olive oil, fruit and vegetables but too little bread, pasta, meat and sugar: the foods of which Greece produces less than 70% of what it uses give 55% of the calories. And the figure flatters Greece, as its pigs and chickens eat feed made of imported soybeans and maize. For a country that sells olive oil, fruit and feta and buys meat, cereals and feed, what matters is to sell enough food to pay for the food it lacks, and in 2025 Greece’s food exports were worth 93% of its food imports.

So, what does it mean?

The Greek economy is one of services, consumption and imports.

  1. Services: trade, transport, hotels and restaurants make 26% of the economy, against 19% in the EU; manufacturing 11%, against 16%.
  2. Consumption: households spend 69% of GDP, the EU’s 53%; investment is 17%, the EU’s 22%.
  3. Trade: Greece sells tourism and shipping, and buys goods: €22.5 billion more services sold than bought, €34.1 billion more goods bought than sold in 2025. Its largest trade in goods is oil, bought crude and sold refined.
  4. Food: about as much sold as bought, in money. Greece produces far more olive oil, fruit and vegetables than it eats, and depends on imports for cereals, meat, fish, sugar and animal feed.

Sources

  • Eurostat: nama_10_a10 (gross value added by industry), nama_10_a10_e (employment by industry), nama_10_gdp (GDP and its uses), bop_its6_det (international trade in services).
  • Eurostat, Comext: DS-045409 (EU trade since 1988 by HS2-4-6 and CN8), through its API.
  • FAOSTAT: Food Balances (2010 onwards).

See also

  • golemeurostat: a Shiny app for exploring the Eurostat indicators of the countries and regions of Europe
