item.title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
item.description: Tourism in Greece in Eurostat data: how many visitors come, when and where they go, where they come from, what they spend and how much Greece depends on them.
item.content:encoded:
Tourism in Greece in Eurostat data: how many visitors come, when and where they go, where they come from, what they spend and how much Greece depends on them.

What is this?

Greece is one of the most visited countries of Europe, and its tourism is squeezed into a few summer months and a few groups of islands. This story follows the tourists through the statistics of Eurostat:

  1. How many come?
  2. When do they come?
  3. Where do they go?
  4. Where do they come from?
  5. How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?
  6. How much does Greece depend on them?
  7. Where do they stay?

The data come from three places, all at Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU:

  • The statistics of tourist accommodation: the nights that guests spend in hotels, rented rooms and apartments, and campsites, each month since 1994, by region and by the country the guests live in. A night is one guest staying one night: a couple on a week’s holiday spend 14 nights. Since 2018 Eurostat also counts the nights booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia and Tripadvisor.
  • The survey of the trips of EU residents, which asks people in every EU country where they travelled and what they spent. It tells what a holiday in Greece costs its visitors, against a holiday in Spain, Italy or Croatia.
  • The balance of payments, which records what foreign visitors spend in each country, so it can be set against the size of its economy.

They are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
# a monthly Eurostat dataset, the same way, with the year and the month of each value
eurostat_months <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "date", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x$year <- as.integer(format(x$time, "%Y"))
  x$month <- as.integer(format(x$time, "%m"))
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
eu <- eu_countries$code
eu_name <- c(setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code), EU27_2020 = "EU-27", TR = "Türkiye")
# Greece every year: the nights at all tourist accommodation (I551-I553), in hotels (I551), in rented
# rooms, apartments and holiday homes (I552, counted from 2009) and in campsites (I553), of all
# guests, of guests from abroad and of Greeks
kinds <- c(I551 = "Hotels", I552 = "Rented rooms and apartments", I553 = "Campsites")
annual <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_ninat", list(
  geo = "EL", unit = "NR", c_resid = c("TOTAL", "FOR", "DOM"), nace_r2 = c("I551-I553", names(kinds))
))
nights <- function(year, kind = "I551-I553", resid = "TOTAL") {
  annual$values[annual$time == year & annual$nace_r2 == kind & annual$c_resid == resid]
}
years <- annual$time[annual$nace_r2 == "I551-I553" & annual$c_resid == "TOTAL"]
year_now <- max(years)
# the nights of each month at all tourist accommodation, every EU country
monthly <- eurostat_months("tour_occ_nim", list(geo = c(eu, "EU27_2020"), unit = "NR", c_resid = "TOTAL", nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
greece <- monthly[monthly$geo == "EL", ]
month_now <- max(greece$time)   # the latest month
full_year <- max(as.integer(names(which(table(greece$year) == 12))))   # the latest year with all twelve months
# the regions of Greece (NUTS 2): the nights of each month since 2020, also per thousand inhabitants,
# of all guests and of guests from abroad
regions <- c(
  EL30 = "Attica", EL41 = "North Aegean", EL42 = "South Aegean", EL43 = "Crete",
  EL51 = "Eastern Macedonia and Thrace", EL52 = "Central Macedonia", EL53 = "Western Macedonia",
  EL54 = "Epirus", EL61 = "Thessaly", EL62 = "Ionian Islands", EL63 = "Western Greece",
  EL64 = "Central Greece", EL65 = "Peloponnese"
)
regional <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_nin2m", list(geo = names(regions), unit = c("NR", "P_THAB"), c_resid = c("TOTAL", "FOR"), nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
region_year <- max(regional$time)
# the nights in Greece by the country the guests live in; countries only, not groups such as EUR
origins <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_ninraw", list(geo = "EL", unit = "NR", nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
origins <- origins[nchar(origins$c_resid) == 2, ]
origin_nights <- function(country, year) origins$values[match(paste(country, year), paste(origins$c_resid, origins$time))]
# the survey of trips: what EU residents spend on holidays (trips for personal purposes of one night or
# more) in each country, by kind of spending, and the number of those trips and of their nights
destinations <- c("EL", "ES", "IT", "PT", "HR", "CY", "MT", "FR", "AT", "BG", "TR")
parts <- c(TRA = "Getting there and around", ACCOM = "Accommodation", OTHER = "Food, drinks and everything else")
survey <- list(geo = c("EU27_2020", setdiff(destinations, "TR")), c_dest = c(destinations, "DOM"), purpose = "PER", duration = "N_GE1")
# all spending (TOTXDUR, without durable goods), on transport and on accommodation; the rest is
# "everything else", as some countries count cafés and restaurants apart and others do not
per_trip <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_extotw", c(survey, list(statinfo = "AVG_TRP", expend = c("TOTXDUR", "TRA", "ACCOM"))))
trips <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_ttw", survey)
trip_nights <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_tnw", survey)
# Eurostat gives the totals of each kind of spending only for the trips at home; for the others they
# are the spending per trip times the trips
spent <- merge(per_trip[c("geo", "c_dest", "time", "expend", "values")], trips[c("geo", "c_dest", "time", "values")],
  by = c("geo", "c_dest", "time"), suffixes = c("_per_trip", "_trips"))
spent$values <- spent$values_per_trip * spent$values_trips
# consumer prices, 2015 = 100, in Greece and in the EU
prices <- eurostat_values("prc_hicp_aind", list(geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), coicop = "CP00", unit = "INX_A_AVG"))
# what foreign visitors spend in each country (travel, in the balance of payments) and GDP, million euros
receipts <- eurostat_values("bop_its6_det", list(geo = c(eu, "TR"), bop_item = "SD", stk_flow = "CRE", partner = "WRL_REST", currency = "MIO_EUR"))
gdp <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(geo = c(eu, "TR"), na_item = "B1GQ", unit = "CP_MEUR"))
# the nights booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia and Tripadvisor, Greece and its regions
platforms <- eurostat_values("tour_ce_omn12", list(geo = c("EL", names(regions)), indic_to = "NGT_SP", c_resid = "TOTAL", month = "TOTAL"))
platform_year <- max(platforms$time)
on_platforms <- function(geo, year = platform_year) platforms$values[platforms$geo == geo & platforms$time == year]
Code 
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels
amber <- "#c97b1e"
# the three parts of a stacked bar, told apart also with colour blindness: light blue, amber, dark blue
stack_colors <- c("#5b8fd6", amber, "#1c5cab")
# a scale from few nights (white) to many (dark blue)
blues <- list(c(0, "#f4f8fd"), c(0.5, "#3987e5"), c(1, "#0d366b"))
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    # at the top, so that a legend of two or three rows fits under it in a larger top margin
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
months <- factor(month.abb, levels = month.abb)   # in this order on an axis
# a horizontal bar chart of countries or regions, from the highest at the top: by default one of
# them in red, the EU in blue and the others in gray
ranking_bars <- function(x, value, highlight, hover,
                         colors = function(x) ifelse(x$geo == highlight, greek_red, ifelse(x$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))) {
  x <- x[order(x[[value]]), ]
  plot_ly(
    y = factor(x$name, levels = x$name), x = x[[value]], type = "bar", orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = colors(x)), hovertext = hover(x), hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
  )
}
# short labels of numbers
million <- function(x, digits = 1) paste(format(round(x / 1e6, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "million")
euros <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE))
billion_euros <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE), " billion")   # from million euros
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
# "A", "A and B", "A, B and C"
and_list <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2) x else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
# the place of a country counted from the highest: 1 is the highest
highest <- function(k) {
  if (k > 8) return(paste0("the ", k, "th highest"))
  paste0("the ", c("", "second ", "third ", "fourth ", "fifth ", "sixth ", "seventh ", "eighth ")[k], "highest")
}

1. How many come?

Code 
record <- years[which.max(sapply(years, nights))]
foreign_share <- function(year) 100 * nights(year, resid = "FOR") / nights(year)
hotels_growth <- 100 * (nights(year_now, "I551") / nights(min(years), "I551") - 1)
covid_fall <- 100 * (1 - nights(2020) / nights(2019))
recovered <- min(years[years > 2020 & sapply(years, nights) > nights(2019)])
# this year so far, against the same months of last year
latest_year <- as.integer(format(month_now, "%Y"))
latest_month <- as.integer(format(month_now, "%m"))
so_far <- function(year) sum(greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month <= latest_month])

156.3 million nights in 2025, more than ever.

In 2025, guests spent 156.3 million nights in the hotels, rented rooms and apartments, and campsites of Greece, 84% of them guests from abroad. Hotels alone had 119.0 million nights, 129% more than in 1994. In the first 8 months of 2026 there were 1.8% more nights than in the same months of 2025.

Until 2008 Greece counted only the nights in hotels and campsites; from 2009 it counts those in rented rooms, apartments and holiday homes too, so the bars jump in 2009. Since then the nights fell twice: in the debt crisis, to 80.6 million in 2012, and in 2020, when COVID closed the borders, by 73%. By 2023 there were more than in 2019.

Code 
kind_colors <- c(I551 = stack_colors[3], I552 = stack_colors[2], I553 = stack_colors[1])
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(kinds)) {
  x <- annual[annual$nace_r2 == k & annual$c_resid == "TOTAL", ]
  p <- add_trace(p,
    x = x$time, y = x$values / 1e6, type = "bar", name = kinds[[k]],
    marker = list(color = kind_colors[[k]], line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>", kinds[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart("Nights at tourist accommodation in Greece, million", "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninat", "Million",
  barmode = "stack", bargap = 0.15, legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "normal"), margin = list(t = 100, b = 90),
  annotations = list(list(x = 2009, y = nights(2009) / 1e6, text = "2009: rented rooms and<br>apartments counted too",
    showarrow = TRUE, ax = -70, ay = -45, font = list(color = dark_gray))))

Interactive chart: Nights at tourist accommodation in Greece, million

More and more of the guests come from abroad: 69% of the nights in 2010, 84% in 2025. In 2020, with few foreigners able to travel, the share fell to 68%.

2. When do they come?

Code 
in_month <- function(year, month) greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month == month]
in_months <- function(year, months) sum(greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month %in% months])
summer <- 6:9
winter <- c(1:3, 11:12)
summer_share <- 100 * in_months(full_year, summer) / in_months(full_year, 1:12)
summer_growth <- in_months(full_year, summer) - in_months(2010, summer)
winter_growth <- in_months(full_year, winter) - in_months(2010, winter)

In August, 21 times as many nights as in January.

In 2025, guests spent 1.6 million nights in Greece in January and 34.0 million in August. 72% of the nights of the year fell in the four months from June to September. Each row of the chart is a year and each cell a month: the darker the cell, the more nights. Greece has added summer, not winter: from 2010 to 2025, the nights from June to September grew by 49.5 million, those from November to March by 4.2 million.

Code 
heat <- greece[greece$year >= 2009, ]
z <- tapply(heat$values / 1e6, list(heat$year, factor(heat$month, levels = 1:12)), sum)   # years in rows, months in columns
plot_ly(
  x = months, y = rownames(z), z = z, type = "heatmap", colorscale = blues, xgap = 2, ygap = 2,
  colorbar = list(title = list(text = "Million<br>nights"), thickness = 12),
  hovertemplate = "%{x} %{y}: %{z:.1f} million nights<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Nights in Greece each month, million",
    paste0("Eurostat, tour_occ_nim, January 2009 to ", month.name[latest_month], " ", latest_year, "; blank: no data"), y_axis = list(type = "category", autorange = "reversed"), note_y = -0.08)

Interactive chart: Nights in Greece each month, million

Code 
season <- monthly[monthly$year == full_year, ]
complete <- names(which(table(season$geo) == 12))
by_season <- data.frame(geo = complete, name = eu_name[complete])
by_season$share <- sapply(complete, function(k) {
  x <- season[season$geo == k, ]
  100 * sum(x$values[x$month %in% summer]) / sum(x$values)
})
season_order <- by_season$geo[by_season$geo != "EU27_2020"][order(-by_season$share[by_season$geo != "EU27_2020"])]
more_seasonal <- season_order[seq_len(match("EL", season_order) - 1)]
eu_share <- by_season$share[by_season$geo == "EU27_2020"]

One of the most seasonal in the EU. In the EU as a whole, 52% of the nights at tourist accommodation fall from June to September; in Greece, 72%. Only Croatia packs more of its tourism into them. Hotels, restaurants and the people who work in them have to earn the year’s living in a few months.

Code 
ranking_bars(by_season, "share", "EL", function(x) paste0(x$name, ": ", percent(x$share, 1), " of the year's nights")) %>%
  chart(paste0("Share of the nights of ", full_year, " spent from June to September, %"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nim",
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.1)

Interactive chart: Share of the nights of 2025 spent from June to September, %

3. Where do they go?

Code 
year_total <- regional[regional$time == region_year & regional$month == "TOTAL", ]
region_value <- function(unit, resid) {
  year_total$values[match(paste(names(regions), unit, resid), paste(year_total$geo, year_total$unit, year_total$c_resid))]
}
by_region <- data.frame(geo = names(regions), name = regions)
by_region$nights <- region_value("NR", "TOTAL")
by_region$per_person <- region_value("P_THAB", "TOTAL") / 1000
by_region$foreign <- 100 * region_value("NR", "FOR") / by_region$nights
islands <- c("EL42", "EL43", "EL62")
islands_foreign <- min(by_region$foreign[by_region$geo %in% islands])
islands_share <- 100 * sum(by_region$nights[by_region$geo %in% islands]) / sum(by_region$nights)
in_region <- function(geo, column) by_region[[column]][by_region$geo == geo]
# the share of the nights of the year that a region has in each month
m <- regional[regional$time == region_year & regional$unit == "NR" & regional$c_resid == "TOTAL" & regional$month != "TOTAL", ]
m$month <- as.integer(sub("M", "", m$month))
by_month <- function(geo) {
  x <- m[m$geo == geo, ]
  x <- x[order(x$month), ]
  100 * x$values / sum(x$values)
}
summer_of <- function(geo) sum(by_month(geo)[summer])

62% of the nights on three groups of islands. In 2025, the South Aegean, the Cyclades and the Dodecanese with Santorini, Mykonos, Rhodes and Kos, had 41.8 million nights; Crete 35.2 million; the Ionian Islands, with Corfu, Zakynthos and Kefalonia, 20.4 million. Attica, with Athens, had 12.8 million. Against the people who live there, the islands are full: 128 nights a year for each inhabitant of the South Aegean and 103 in the Ionian Islands, against 3.4 in Attica. On the islands, 91% or more of the nights are those of guests from abroad.

Code 
by_region$million_nights <- by_region$nights / 1e6
ranking_bars(by_region, "million_nights", "", function(x) {
  paste0(x$name, ": ", million(x$nights), " nights, ", round(x$per_person, 1), " per inhabitant, ", percent(x$foreign), " from abroad")
}, colors = function(x) ifelse(x$geo %in% islands, blue, gray)) %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights at tourist accommodation by region, ", region_year, ", million"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m",
    margin = list(l = 200, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Nights at tourist accommodation by region, 2025, million

Athens works all year, the islands in the summer. 80% of the nights of the Ionian Islands and 74% of those of the South Aegean fall from June to September, against 49% in Attica, where city breaks, business and conferences fill the hotels in spring and autumn too.

Code 
shown <- c(EL62 = amber, EL42 = stack_colors[3], EL43 = stack_colors[1], EL30 = gray)
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(shown)) {
  p <- add_trace(p,
    x = months, y = by_month(k), type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = regions[[k]],
    line = list(color = shown[[k]], width = if (k == "EL30") 2 else 3, dash = if (k == "EL30") "dash" else "solid"),
    marker = list(color = shown[[k]], size = 8),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of the year<extra>", regions[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart(paste0("Share of the nights of ", region_year, " in each month, %"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m", "% of the year",
  y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top, margin = list(t = 100, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Share of the nights of 2025 in each month, %

4. Where do they come from?

Code 
origin_year <- max(origins$time)
latest <- origins[origins$time == origin_year, ]
latest <- latest[order(-latest$values), ]
latest$name <- as.character(label_eurostat(latest$c_resid, dic = "c_resid"))
latest$name[latest$c_resid == "EL"] <- "Greece (Greeks at home)"
abroad <- latest[latest$c_resid != "EL", ]
# a country's name in a sentence: "the United Kingdom"
in_text <- function(name) ifelse(name %in% c("United Kingdom", "United States", "Netherlands"), paste("the", name), name)
share_of_foreign <- function(country) 100 * origin_nights(country, origin_year) / nights(origin_year, resid = "FOR")
change <- function(country, from = 2019) origin_nights(country, origin_year) - origin_nights(country, from)

Most come from the United Kingdom and Germany. In 2025, guests from the United Kingdom spent 25.4 million nights in Greece and those from Germany 21.0 million: together 35% of the nights of guests from abroad. Greeks on holiday in their own country spent 25.3 million.

The list has changed since 2019. The Russians, who spent 6.6 million nights in Greece in 2019, have almost gone since the EU closed its skies to Russian planes in 2022: 0.36 million in 2025. The Americans came in their place: 6.1 million nights, against 3.9 million in 2019. Poland and Romania grew too, by 1.3 million and 1.9 million nights.

Code 
top <- head(latest, 12)
top <- top[order(top$values), ]
plot_ly(
  y = factor(top$name, levels = top$name), x = top$values / 1e6, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(top$c_resid == "EL", gray, blue)),
  hovertext = paste0(top$name, ": ", million(top$values), " nights in ", origin_year, ", ",
    million(origin_nights(top$c_resid, 2019)), " in 2019"),
  hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights in Greece by the country of the guests, ", origin_year, ", million"),
    "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninraw", margin = list(l = 190, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Nights in Greece by the country of the guests, 2025, million

5. How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?

Eurostat’s survey of trips asks people in every EU country where they went on holiday and what it cost them. The trips to a country include those of its own people on holiday at home, which are cheaper, as there is no long journey: so they are taken out here, and what remains are the visitors from the other EU countries. Türkiye, outside the EU, is in the comparison as Greece’s nearest competitor; all its visitors in the survey come from abroad.

Code 
# the value for the visitors to a country from the other EU countries: all EU residents, minus its
# own residents on holiday at home (Türkiye has none in the survey)
from_abroad <- function(x, country, year) {
  everyone <- x$values[x$geo == "EU27_2020" & x$c_dest == country & x$time == year]
  at_home <- if (country == "TR") 0 else x$values[x$geo == country & x$c_dest == "DOM" & x$time == year]
  if (length(everyone) != 1 || length(at_home) != 1) return(NA)
  everyone - at_home
}
spending <- function(year) {
  x <- data.frame(geo = destinations, name = eu_name[destinations])
  for (p in c("TOTXDUR", "TRA", "ACCOM")) x[[p]] <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(spent[spent$expend == p, ], d, year))
  x$OTHER <- x$TOTXDUR - x$TRA - x$ACCOM
  x$trips <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(trips, d, year))
  x$nights <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(trip_nights, d, year))
  x$per_trip <- x$TOTXDUR / x$trips
  x$per_night <- x$per_trip * x$trips / x$nights
  x$length <- x$nights / x$trips
  x[!is.na(x$per_trip), ]
}
survey_year <- max(trips$time[trips$geo == "EU27_2020" & trips$c_dest == "EL"])
costs <- spending(survey_year)
cost <- function(geo, column = "per_trip") costs[[column]][costs$geo == geo]
part_cost <- function(geo, part) cost(geo, part) / cost(geo, "trips")
by_trip <- costs$geo[order(-costs$per_trip)]
by_night <- costs$geo[order(-costs$per_night)]
by_length <- costs$geo[order(-costs$length)]
# the countries ahead of Greece in a ranking
before_greece <- function(ranking) ranking[seq_len(match("EL", ranking) - 1)]

A holiday in Greece costs its visitors €1,256, the third highest of the 11 holiday countries in the chart.

In 2025, visitors from the other EU countries spent €1,256 on a holiday trip to Greece, against €1,152 in Spain, €970 in Italy and €888 in Croatia; only Cyprus and Türkiye cost more. The money includes the journey: €379 of it went on getting there and around, mostly on the flights; €436 on accommodation; and €441 on food, drinks and everything else.

Code 
costs <- costs[order(costs$per_trip), ]
labels <- ifelse(costs$geo == "EL", "<b>Greece</b>", costs$name)
y <- factor(labels, levels = labels)
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in seq_along(parts)) {
  p <- add_trace(p,
    y = y, x = costs[[names(parts)[k]]] / costs$trips, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = parts[[k]],
    marker = list(color = stack_colors[k], line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: €%{x:,.0f}<extra>", parts[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart(paste0("What a holiday trip costs, ", survey_year, ", euros"),
  "Eurostat, tour_dem_extotw and tour_dem_ttw: visitors from the other EU countries; own calculation",
  x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.15 * max(costs$per_trip))),
  barmode = "stack", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "normal"), margin = list(l = 110, t = 100, b = 90),
  annotations = lapply(seq_len(nrow(costs)), function(k) {
    list(x = costs$per_trip[k], y = labels[k], text = euros(costs$per_trip[k]), xanchor = "left", xshift = 4,
      showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))
  }))

Interactive chart: What a holiday trip costs, 2025, euros

Per night, too, Greece is among the dearest. Visitors stay long in Greece, 8.6 nights a trip (only in Türkiye and Spain do they stay longer), so the cost of the flight is spread over more nights. A night of holiday in Greece costs them €145, the third highest of the 11: Cyprus (€173) and Malta (€163) cost more.

Code 
ranking_bars(costs, "per_night", "EL", function(x) {
  paste0(x$name, ": ", euros(x$per_night), " a night, ", one(x$length), " nights a trip")
}) %>%
  chart(paste0("What a night of holiday costs, ", survey_year, ", euros"),
    "Eurostat, tour_dem_extotw and tour_dem_tnw: visitors from the other EU countries; own calculation",
    margin = list(l = 110, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: What a night of holiday costs, 2025, euros

Code 
trip_cost <- function(year) {
  x <- spending(year)
  x$per_trip[x$geo == "EL"]
}
price_year <- min(survey_year, max(prices$time))
price_change <- function(geo) 100 * (prices$values[prices$geo == geo & prices$time == price_year] / prices$values[prices$geo == geo & prices$time == 2019] - 1)
cost_change <- 100 * (trip_cost(survey_year) / trip_cost(2019) - 1)
real_change <- c(100 * ((1 + cost_change / 100) / (1 + price_change("EL") / 100) - 1),
                 100 * ((1 + cost_change / 100) / (1 + price_change("EU27_2020") / 100) - 1))
# within 5% of 2019 after inflation, by the prices of Greece and of the EU, is "about the same"
real_spending <- if (all(abs(real_change) < 5)) "about the same" else if (all(real_change > 0)) "more" else if (all(real_change < 0)) "less" else "about the same"

More visitors, not richer ones. In 2019, a holiday trip to Greece cost visitors from the other EU countries €1,025; in 2025, €1,256, 23% more. Consumer prices rose by 20% in Greece and by 26% in the EU over the same years, so after inflation each visitor spends about what they spent in 2019: what has grown is the number of visitors. The survey asks a sample of people, so the figure of a single year can jump: it is the change over several years that counts.

6. How much does Greece depend on them?

Code 
both <- merge(receipts[c("geo", "time", "values")], gdp[c("geo", "time", "values")], by = c("geo", "time"), suffixes = c("_receipts", "_gdp"))
both$share <- 100 * both$values_receipts / both$values_gdp
receipts_year <- max(both$time[both$geo == "EL"])
share_of <- function(geo, year = receipts_year) both$share[both$geo == geo & both$time == year]
earned <- function(geo, year = receipts_year) both$values_receipts[both$geo == geo & both$time == year]
dependence <- both[both$time == receipts_year, ]
dependence$name <- eu_name[dependence$geo]
by_share <- dependence$geo[order(-dependence$share)]
ahead_of_greece <- by_share[seq_len(match("EL", by_share) - 1)]

€23.6 billion in 2025, 9.5% of GDP. That is what visitors from abroad spent in Greece, on hotels, meals, transport and shopping, without the flights to get there. Of the countries in the chart, only Croatia (16.3%), Malta (12.1%) and Cyprus (10.9%) depend more on them; in Spain they spent 6.2% of GDP, in Italy 2.5%. The figure counts only what foreigners spend: the holidays of Greeks at home, and the farms, builders and shops that sell to hotels, add to what the economy owes to tourism.

Code 
ranking_bars(dependence, "share", "EL", function(x) paste0(x$name, ": ", percent(x$share, 1), " of GDP, ", billion_euros(x$values_receipts))) %>%
  chart(paste0("What visitors from abroad spend, ", receipts_year, ", % of GDP"),
    "Eurostat, bop_its6_det (travel, credit) and nama_10_gdp", margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.1)

Interactive chart: What visitors from abroad spend, 2025, % of GDP

What a country depends on, it can lose. In 2020 visitors from abroad spent €4.3 billion in Greece, 2.6% of GDP, against €18.2 billion in 2019.

Code 
greek <- both[both$geo == "EL", ]
plot_ly(greek,
  x = ~time, y = ~share, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Greece",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 8),
  hovertext = paste0(greek$time, ": ", percent(greek$share, 1), " of GDP, ", billion_euros(greek$values_receipts)),
  hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("What visitors from abroad spend in Greece, % of GDP", "Eurostat, bop_its6_det (travel, credit) and nama_10_gdp",
    "% of GDP", y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"))

Interactive chart: What visitors from abroad spend in Greece, % of GDP

7. Where do they stay?

Code 
compare_year <- min(platform_year, year_now)
platform_growth <- 100 * (on_platforms("EL", compare_year) / on_platforms("EL", 2019) - 1)
registered_growth <- 100 * (nights(compare_year) / nights(2019) - 1)
platforms_grew_more <- on_platforms("EL", compare_year) - on_platforms("EL", 2019) > nights(compare_year) - nights(2019)
stay_year <- min(platform_year, region_year)
stays <- regional[regional$time == stay_year & regional$month == "TOTAL" & regional$unit == "NR" & regional$c_resid == "TOTAL", ]
by_region$registered <- stays$values[match(by_region$geo, stays$geo)]
by_region$platforms <- sapply(by_region$geo, on_platforms, year = stay_year)
by_region$per_100 <- 100 * by_region$platforms / by_region$registered
platforms_per_100 <- function(geo) by_region$per_100[by_region$geo == geo]
more_than_attica <- by_region$name[by_region$per_100 > platforms_per_100("EL30")]

More and more of them in flats let through Airbnb and the like. In 2025, guests spent 52.1 million nights in places booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia or Tripadvisor, 115% more than in 2019. The nights in hotels, rented rooms and campsites grew by 9% in the same years. Some places are listed on the platforms and also counted as tourist accommodation, so the two cannot simply be added; but the platforms gained 27.8 million nights since 2019, the tourist accommodation 12.8 million: most of the growth has gone to the platforms.

Code 
since <- min(platforms$time)
registered <- data.frame(time = since:year_now)
registered$values <- sapply(registered$time, nights)
greek_platforms <- platforms[platforms$geo == "EL", ]
plot_ly(registered,
  x = ~time, y = ~ values / 1e6, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Hotels, rented rooms and campsites",
  line = list(color = blue, width = 3), marker = list(color = blue, size = 8),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>Tourist accommodation</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = greek_platforms, x = ~time, y = ~ values / 1e6, name = "Booked through the platforms",
    line = list(color = amber, width = 3), marker = list(color = amber, size = 8),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>Platforms</extra>", inherit = FALSE,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers") %>%
  chart("Nights in Greece, million", "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninat and tour_ce_omn12 (Airbnb, Booking, Expedia, Tripadvisor)",
    "Million", y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: Nights in Greece, million

In Athens, 81 nights on the platforms for every 100 in tourist accommodation. That is what Attica had in 2025, more than any other region; the South Aegean had 22 and Crete 25. Many of the flats let to visitors in Athens were once let to people who live there, which is one reason given for the rise of rents in the city; the story of Greek housing follows rents and house prices against incomes.

Code 
x <- by_region[order(by_region$registered), ]
y <- factor(x$name, levels = x$name)
plot_ly(
  y = y, x = x$registered / 1e6, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = "Hotels, rented rooms and campsites",
  marker = list(color = blue), hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f} million nights<extra>Tourist accommodation</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(y = y, x = x$platforms / 1e6, name = "Booked through the platforms", marker = list(color = amber),
    hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f} million nights<extra>Platforms</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights by region, ", stay_year, ", million"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m and tour_ce_omn12",
    barmode = "group", legend = legend_top, margin = list(l = 200, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.12)

Interactive chart: Nights by region, 2025, million

So, what does it mean?

Tourism is one of the pillars of the Greek economy, and one of its risks. Visitors from abroad spend 9.5% of GDP in Greece, and they spend it:

  1. In the summer: 72% of the nights fall from June to September. Greece has grown its summers, not its winters, so jobs and incomes in tourism remain seasonal.
  2. On the islands: 62% of the nights are spent in the South Aegean, Crete and the Ionian Islands, where there are 128 nights for each inhabitant of the South Aegean every year, with what that means for water, roads and housing in August.
  3. On long trips: a holiday in Greece costs its visitors from the rest of the EU €1,256, the third highest of the 11 holiday countries in the chart, and a night €145, the third highest. After inflation, each visitor spends about as much as before COVID: the growth comes from more visitors.
  4. Through the platforms: since 2019, nights booked through Airbnb and the like grew by 115%, the registered tourist accommodation by 9%.

2020 showed the risk: when the visitors could not come, 73% of the nights were lost in one year. Longer seasons, more regions and more visitors from outside Europe would spread it.

Sources

  • Eurostat, tourist accommodation: tour_occ_ninat (nights per year), tour_occ_nim (nights per month), tour_occ_nin2m (nights by month and region), tour_occ_ninraw (nights by the country of the guests), tour_ce_omn12 (short-stay accommodation booked through online platforms).
  • Eurostat, trips of EU residents: tour_dem_extotw (expenditure per trip by destination), tour_dem_ttw (trips by destination), tour_dem_tnw (nights by destination).
  • Eurostat, economy: bop_its6_det (international trade in services: travel), nama_10_gdp (GDP), prc_hicp_aind (consumer prices).

See also

  • golemeurostat: a Shiny app for exploring the Eurostat indicators of the countries and regions of Europe

item.title: Fewer and Older: Greece’s Population, Its Economy and Its Debt
item.description: Greece’s shrinking and ageing population in Eurostat projections, and what fewer workers mean for growth, pensions, health spending and the public debt.
item.content:encoded:
Greece’s shrinking and ageing population in Eurostat projections, and what fewer workers mean for growth, pensions, health spending and the public debt.

What is this?

Greece has had fewer people every year since 2011. The official projections say that the fall will go on for the rest of the century, and that the people will be older. This story asks what that means for the economy, and for the public debt that the economy has to carry:

  1. How many people will Greece have?
  2. Why is the population falling?
  3. How old will it be?
  4. Who will work, and how much will they produce?
  5. What will pensions and health care cost?
  6. What happens to the debt?

The data come from two places:

  • Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU: the population since 1960, births, deaths, migration, employment, productivity and the debt, and EUROPOP2023, its projections of the population of every EU country to 2100. They are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures.
  • The European Commission’s 2024 Ageing Report, which projects what pensions, health care, long-term care and education will cost in each EU country until 2070, with the same population projections, and how fast each economy can grow. The report is a PDF, so its figures are typed in below, with the table they come from.

A projection is not a forecast. EUROPOP2023 starts from the population of 2022 and shows what happens if births, deaths and migration follow the paths that Eurostat assumed in 2023. Besides this baseline, it has variants, with more or fewer migrants, none at all, fewer births or longer lives, which show how much the result depends on these assumptions.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
# one series of a dataset, in the order of the years
by_year <- function(x, years) x$values[match(years, x$time)]
# Greece since 1960: the population on 1 January, births, deaths and net migration
# (with the statistical adjustment that makes the population of each year add up)
balance <- eurostat_values("demo_gind", list(geo = "EL", indic_de = c("JAN", "LBIRTH", "DEATH", "CNMIGRAT")))
history <- data.frame(year = sort(unique(balance$time)))
history$population <- by_year(balance[balance$indic_de == "JAN", ], history$year)
history$births <- by_year(balance[balance$indic_de == "LBIRTH", ], history$year)
history$deaths <- by_year(balance[balance$indic_de == "DEATH", ], history$year)
history$net_migration <- by_year(balance[balance$indic_de == "CNMIGRAT", ], history$year)
now <- max(history$year[!is.na(history$population)])   # the latest population
last <- max(history$year[!is.na(history$births)])      # the latest year of births and deaths
past <- function(column, year) history[[column]][history$year == year]
peak <- max(history$population, na.rm = TRUE)
peak_year <- history$year[which.max(history$population)]
# children per woman, every country
fertility <- eurostat_values("demo_find", list(indic_de = "TOTFERRT"))
# the age groups of this story
groups <- c(young = "Under 20", working = "20 to 64", old = "65 to 79", oldest = "80 and over")
# the age of a Eurostat age code: Y_LT1 is under one, Y_OPEN and Y_GE100 are the oldest,
# and the codes of totals, such as TOTAL, give NA
age_of <- function(code) {
  age <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("^Y", "", code)))
  age[code == "Y_LT1"] <- 0
  age[code %in% c("Y_OPEN", "Y_GE100")] <- 100
  age
}
# the people of each age group by year, from a dataset by single year of age
by_age_group <- function(x) {
  x$age <- age_of(x$age)
  x <- x[!is.na(x$age), ]
  x$group <- cut(x$age, c(-1, 19, 64, 79, Inf), labels = names(groups))
  counts <- aggregate(values ~ time + group, x, sum)
  wide <- reshape(counts, idvar = "time", timevar = "group", direction = "wide")
  names(wide) <- sub("^values\\.", "", names(wide))
  names(wide)[names(wide) == "time"] <- "year"
  wide$total <- rowSums(wide[names(groups)])
  wide[order(wide$year), ]
}
# Greece by age group since 1980, as earlier years lack the single years of age
ages_past <- by_age_group(eurostat_values("demo_pjan", list(geo = "EL", sex = "T")))
ages_past <- ages_past[ages_past$year >= 1980, ]
ages_now <- max(ages_past$year)
age_past <- function(column, year = ages_now) ages_past[[column]][ages_past$year == year]
# EUROPOP2023: Greece by age group until 2100, in the baseline and its variants
variants <- c(
  BSL = "Baseline", HMIGR = "Higher migration", LMIGR = "Lower migration",

    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.2f} million<extra>", paths$label[k], "</extra>"), inherit = FALSE
  )
}
p %>% chart("People aged 20 to 64 in work, million, at three employment rates",
  "Eurostat, lfsi_emp_a and proj_23np (EUROPOP2023, baseline); own calculation", "Million",
  shapes = list(projection_start(job_year)), annotations = c(
    list(projection_label(job_year)),
    end_labels(2075, sapply(workers, function(w) w[length(w)]) / 1e6, percent(paths$rate))
  ),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90, r = 60), legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: People aged 20 to 64 in work, million, at three employment rates

Code 
fewer_in_2050 <- function(key) 100 * (1 - workers[[key]][years_ahead == 2050] / jobs_now)

If the employment rate stays at 71%, Greece has 28% fewer workers in 2050 than in 2025; at the EU’s 76%, 23% fewer. Even at 80%, a rate that 10 EU countries already have, it has 19% fewer.

Productivity that does not grow

Code 
productivity_year <- max(productivity$time)
since_2000 <- function(geo) productivity$index[productivity$geo == geo & productivity$time == productivity_year] - 100

What each worker produces has not grown in a quarter of a century. Output per person employed, after inflation, rose fast in Greece until 2008, fell in the crisis and is recovering, but in 2025 it was 4% lower than in 2000. In the EU it was 20% higher.

Code 
plot_ly(productivity[productivity$geo == "EL", ],
  x = ~time, y = ~index, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Greece",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}<extra>Greece</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = productivity[productivity$geo == "EU27_2020", ], x = ~time, y = ~index, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    name = "EU-27", line = list(color = blue, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}<extra>EU-27</extra>", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart("Output per person employed, after inflation, 2000 = 100", "Eurostat, nama_10_lp_ulc (real labour productivity per person)",
    "2000 = 100", legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: Output per person employed, after inflation, 2000 = 100

What it means for the economy

Code 
# GDP and the debt ratio year by year, from the last year of the debt to 2070. GDP grows with the
# number of people aged 20 to 64 who work and with what each of them produces (the people at work
# over 64 are left out); section 6 explains the debt.
debt_now <- debt("GD", "PC_GDP")
start_rate <- debt("D41PAY", "MIO_EUR") / debt("GD", "MIO_EUR", debt_year - 1)   # interest paid / debt a year earlier
rate_to <- 0.03       # the average interest rate on the debt in ten years
inflation <- 0.02     # a year
surplus <- 2.5        # the primary surplus, % of GDP
project <- function(productivity = 0.01, variant = "BSL", employment_to = rate_eu, shrink = TRUE, extra_pensions = FALSE) {
  years <- debt_year:2070
  people <- future[future$projection == variant, ]
  working <- people$working[match(years, people$year)]
  if (!shrink) working[] <- working[1]
  in_work <- working * rate_path(years, employment_to)
  real_growth <- in_work[-1] / in_work[-length(in_work)] * (1 + productivity) - 1
  growth <- (1 + real_growth) * (1 + inflation) - 1
  k <- seq_along(growth)
  interest <- start_rate + (rate_to - start_rate) * pmin(1, k / 10)
  primary <- rep(surplus, length(k))
  if (extra_pensions) primary <- primary - approx(constant_benefit$year, constant_benefit$extra, years[-1])$y
  ratio <- debt_now
  for (j in k) ratio[j + 1] <- ratio[j] * (1 + interest[j]) / (1 + growth[j]) - primary[j]
  gdp <- 100 * cumprod(c(1, 1 + real_growth))
  population <- people$total[match(years, people$year)]
  data.frame(year = years, gdp = gdp, gdp_person = gdp * population[1] / population, debt_gdp = ratio)
}
scenarios <- list(
  baseline = list(),
  no_fall = list(shrink = FALSE),
  fast = list(productivity = 0.016),
  flat = list(productivity = 0),
  more_migration = list(variant = "HMIGR"),
  no_migration = list(variant = "NMIGR"),
  rate_stays = list(employment_to = rate_now),
  rate_high = list(employment_to = rate_high),
  pensions = list(extra_pensions = TRUE)
)
scenario_names <- c(
  baseline = "Baseline: productivity +1% a year",
  no_fall = "The number of people aged 20 to 64 does not fall",
  fast = "Productivity +1.6% a year, as the Commission assumes",
  flat = "Productivity does not grow, as since 2000",
  more_migration = "Higher migration (EUROPOP2023 variant)",
  no_migration = "No migration (EUROPOP2023 variant)",
  rate_stays = paste("The employment rate stays at", percent(rate_now)),
  rate_high = paste0("The employment rate reaches ", rate_high, "%"),
  pensions = "Pensions keep their value against wages"
)
results <- lapply(scenarios, function(arguments) do.call(project, arguments))
at <- function(name, column, year) results[[name]][[column]][results[[name]]$year == year]
# the scenarios of the charts
lines <- data.frame(
  key = c("fast", "baseline", "flat", "no_fall"),
  label = c("Productivity +1.6% a year", "Productivity +1% a year", "Productivity flat", "+1%, with no fall in the people aged 20 to 64"),
  color = c(blue, greek_red, gray, dark_gray),
  dash = c("solid", "solid", "solid", "dash")
)
scenario_lines <- function(p, column, hover) {
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(lines))) {
    r <- results[[lines$key[k]]]
    p <- add_trace(p,
      x = r$year, y = r[[column]], type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = lines$label[k],
      line = list(color = lines$color[k], width = if (lines$key[k] == "baseline") 3 else 2, dash = lines$dash[k]),
      hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: ", hover, "<extra>", lines$label[k], "</extra>"), inherit = FALSE
    )
  }
  p
}
# the growth of productivity that keeps GDP as it is until 2050, at an employment rate, % a year
needed <- function(to) {
  ratio <- workers_path(to)[years_ahead == 2050] / jobs_now
  100 * (ratio^(-1 / (2050 - job_year)) - 1)
}

To keep the economy from shrinking, what each worker produces has to grow as fast as the number of workers falls: by 1.1% a year until 2050 if the employment rate reaches the EU’s, by 1.3% if it stays as it is. The European Commission assumes, in its Ageing Report, that productivity in Greece will grow by 1.6% a year until 2070, faster than in the EU (1.4%), while the hours worked fall by 0.6% a year, so that GDP grows by 1.1% a year, against 1.3% in the EU. All of Greece’s growth would come from productivity, growing for decades at a pace that it reached only in the years before 2008.

The chart follows GDP after inflation, with the employment rate reaching the EU’s in ten years, at three speeds of productivity; the dashed line shows what would happen if the number of people aged 20 to 64 did not fall:

Code 
scenario_lines(plot_ly(), "gdp", "%{y:.0f}") %>%
  chart(paste0("GDP after inflation, ", debt_year, " = 100"),
    "Eurostat, proj_23np (EUROPOP2023, baseline) and lfsi_emp_a; own scenarios", paste0(debt_year, " = 100"),
    legend = legend_top, margin = list(t = 100, b = 90))

Interactive chart: GDP after inflation, 2025 = 100

With productivity growing by 1% a year, GDP in 2050 is 99 (2025 = 100); if productivity does not grow, 77; at the 1.6% of the Commission, 114. Had the people aged 20 to 64 not been falling, the 1% would have taken it to 137.

A smaller economy is not necessarily a poorer one, as there are fewer people to share it: with productivity growing by 1% a year, GDP per person in 2050 is 14% higher than in 2025. But the debt does not shrink with the population, and the cost of an older population grows: both weigh more on a smaller economy.

5. What will pensions and health care cost?

Greece spends more on pensions than almost any EU country: 14.5% of GDP in 2022, against 11.4% in the EU. With many more older people for each person of working age, one would expect that to rise steeply. The Commission projects that it will not: 14.0% of GDP in 2050 and 12.0% in 2070, the largest fall in the EU.

Code 
reversed <- merge(constant_benefit, ageing[c("year", "pensions")])
plot_ly(ageing,
  x = ~year, y = ~pensions, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Greece",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 8),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Greece</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = reversed, x = ~year, y = ~ pensions + extra, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
    name = "Greece, if pensions keep their value against wages", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 2, dash = "dash"),
    marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 8, symbol = "circle-open"),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Pensions keep their value</extra>", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  add_trace(data = ageing, x = ~year, y = ~pensions_eu, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "EU",
    line = list(color = blue, width = 3), marker = list(color = blue, size = 8),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>EU</extra>", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart("Public spending on pensions, % of GDP, projected",
    "European Commission, 2024 Ageing Report, Table II.1.64; Greek pension fiche, Table 17", "% of GDP",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: Public spending on pensions, % of GDP, projected

Why? The Greek pension fiche of the report breaks the change from 2022 to 2070 down (Table 8):

  • Ageing alone would add 7.7 points of GDP.
  • Smaller pensions against wages take 6.6 points off. Pensions rise with prices, while wages rise with prices and productivity, so the average pension falls from 76.4% of the average wage in 2022 to 57.1% in 2050 and 53.0% in 2070 (in the EU, from 43.2% to 35.8%).
  • More people in work take 2.2 points off.
  • Fewer people retiring early, as the retirement age follows life expectancy, take 0.7 points off.

These are the effects of the reforms of the 2010s. Their price is that each pensioner gets less against the wages of the time, and that is also their risk: if governments raise pensions with wages instead, to keep the benefit ratio of 2022, the report calculates that pensions would cost 2.8 points of GDP more in 2050 and 3.5 more in 2070 — more than the primary surplus assumed in the next section.

Health care costs more as people grow older, but the report expects only a small rise in Greece: from 5.4% of GDP in 2022 to 6.0% in 2050. Long-term care, for those who can no longer look after themselves, costs the Greek state almost nothing, 0.1% of GDP, against 1.7% in the EU, as families give most of it. With 1.19 million people aged 80 and over in 2050, against 0.74 million in 2025, and fewer children for each of them, that will be harder.

Altogether, the report puts what Greece spends on pensions, health care, long-term care and education at 23.4% of GDP in 2022 and 21.0% in 2070, while in the EU it rises from 24.4% to 25.6%. On paper, the cost of ageing is under control in Greece; in practice, that depends on pensions falling behind wages for decades.

6. What happens to the debt?

The debt ratio of next year is this year’s, grown by the interest rate and shrunk by the growth of GDP in euros, minus the primary surplus, the budget before interest:

\[d_{t} = d_{t-1} \times \frac{1 + i_t}{1 + g_t} - pb_t\]

The growth of GDP in euros is the growth of the number of workers, plus the growth of what each of them produces, plus inflation. A shrinking workforce takes something off it every year, so the debt shrinks more slowly against GDP.

The scenarios start from the debt of 2025, 145.4% of GDP, and assume, unless stated otherwise:

  • the people aged 20 to 64 of the baseline projection, of whom 71% work in 2025, rising to the EU’s 76% in ten years;
  • output per worker growing by 1% a year;
  • inflation of 2% a year, the target of the European Central Bank;
  • an average interest rate on the debt rising from 2.1% to 3% in ten years, as cheap loans are replaced by new borrowing at market rates;
  • a primary surplus of 2.5% of GDP every year, as in the steady scenario of the story on the Greek debt.

They are illustrations of how the population affects the debt, not forecasts.

Code 
actual <- edp[edp$na_item == "GD" & edp$unit == "PC_GDP" & edp$time >= 2010, ]
plot_ly(actual,
  x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Actual",
  line = list(color = "black", width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Actual</extra>"
) %>%
  scenario_lines("debt_gdp", "%{y:.0f}% of GDP") %>%
  chart("Greek government debt to 2070, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1, proj_23np and lfsi_emp_a; own scenarios",
    "% of GDP", y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top, margin = list(t = 120, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Greek government debt to 2070, % of GDP

The same scenarios and more, each changing one assumption of the baseline:

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  scenario_names[names(results)],
  sapply(names(results), function(s) round(at(s, "gdp", 2050))),
  sapply(names(results), function(s) percent(at(s, "debt_gdp", 2035))),
  sapply(names(results), function(s) percent(at(s, "debt_gdp", 2050))),
  sapply(names(results), function(s) percent(at(s, "debt_gdp", 2070)))
), col.names = c("Scenario", paste0("GDP in 2050 (", debt_year, " = 100)"), "Debt in 2035", "Debt in 2050", "Debt in 2070"),
row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
Scenario GDP in 2050 (2025 = 100) Debt in 2035 Debt in 2050 Debt in 2070
Baseline: productivity +1% a year 99 121% 108% 67%
The number of people aged 20 to 64 does not fall 137 106% 69% 19%
Productivity +1.6% a year, as the Commission assumes 114 113% 89% 37%
Productivity does not grow, as since 2000 77 135% 150% 143%
Higher migration (EUROPOP2023 variant) 104 118% 101% 55%
No migration (EUROPOP2023 variant) 100 118% 106% 72%
The employment rate stays at 71% 92 131% 120% 80%
The employment rate reaches 80% 104 114% 100% 58%
Pensions keep their value against wages 99 122% 134% 169%
Code 
debt_in <- function(name, year = 2050) round(at(name, "debt_gdp", year))
  • The shrinking population slows the fall of the debt. With productivity growing by 1% a year, the debt falls to 108% of GDP in 2050. If the people aged 20 to 64 did not fall, the same budget would bring it to 69%: the fall in the population costs about 39 points of GDP of debt by 2050.
  • Productivity decides. At 1.6% a year, as the Commission assumes, the debt is 89% of GDP in 2050. If productivity does not grow, as since 2000, it is 150% in 2050 and 143% in 2070: the debt stops falling, even with a primary surplus every year.
  • Migration helps, slowly: with the higher migration of the EUROPOP2023 variant, the debt is 101% of GDP in 2050 and 55% in 2070; with no migration at all, 106% and 72%. As the baseline assumes that a few more people leave than come until 2033, no migration at all does little harm at first.
  • So do more people in work: 100% if the employment rate reaches 80%, 120% if it stays at 71%.
  • Pensions are the largest risk of policy: if they keep their value against wages, and nothing else changes, the debt is 169% of GDP in 2070, instead of 67%.

So, what does it mean?

Greece will still be here in 2075, smaller and older: about 7.6 million people in the baseline projection, fewer than in 1960, and 33% of them aged 65 or over. A smaller population is not by itself a disaster: what matters for the economy and for the debt is how many people work, and what they produce.

  1. Productivity matters most. Output per worker has to grow by about 1.1% a year just to keep GDP from shrinking, and it has not grown since 2000. Between flat productivity and the 1.6% that the Commission assumes lie 61 points of GDP of debt in 2050.
  2. More people in work: fewer Greek women and fewer people over 55 work than in the rest of the EU, which leaves room to grow.
  3. Migration has already given Greece 100,000 more people than projected, and of all the variants of the projection it is the one that changes the population most.
  4. Pensions: the reforms keep the cost of ageing down by letting pensions fall behind wages. Undoing that would cost up to 4.0 points of GDP a year.
  5. Births take the longest: a child born today starts working in about twenty years, so more births would add workers only from the late 2040s.

The debt can keep falling while the population shrinks, but more slowly, and only if productivity grows: the one thing Greece has not managed since 2000.

Economic and Budgetary Projections for the EU Member States (2022-2070), Institutional Paper 279, April 2024 (Tables II.1.64, II.1.79, II.1.107, II.1.114, II.1.131 and II.1.135), and its pension fiche for Greece, prepared by the National Actuarial Authority (Tables 8 and 17).

item.title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
item.description: Greek public debt in Eurostat, World Bank and ESM data: how much Greece owes and to whom, how it compares with the economy and the EU, and whether it can repay.
item.content:encoded:
Greek public debt in Eurostat, World Bank and ESM data: how much Greece owes and to whom, how it compares with the economy and the EU, and whether it can repay.

What is this?

Greece went through one of the deepest debt crises of any modern European economy. More than fifteen years after the first bailout, this story answers four questions with official data:

  1. Does Greece owe more now than in 2010?
  2. Whom does it owe?
  3. How much is that compared with the size of the economy, and with the rest of the EU?
  4. Will Greece be able to repay?

The data come from three places:

  • Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU: the debt, the deficit, the interest, who holds the debt and when it falls due. They are downloaded when the page is rendered, so a new render brings in the latest figures.
  • The World Bank: interest payments as a share of the government’s revenue, back to 1972.
  • The Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) of Greece: who the creditors are, from its Annual Debt Bulletin 2025. The bulletin is a PDF, so its figures are typed in below, with the page they come from.

It follows two other stories of this site: Greece Since 2000 goes through the boom, the crisis and the recovery of the economy, and Same Crisis, Different Endings compares Greece with the other countries of the euro crisis; this one follows the debt.

Two measures of the same debt. Eurostat and the EU count the debt of the whole general government (the State, public bodies, local government and the pension funds) and leave out what one public body owes another: that is the figure of the EU rules, and of the headlines. The PDMA also reports the debt of the State alone, which includes the short-term loans that other public bodies make to the State with their spare cash. At the end of 2025 the first was €362.9 billion, the second €406.2 billion. This story uses the first, except where it names the creditors of the State.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
}
# debt, deficit and interest of the general government of Greece
edp <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list(
  geo = "EL", sector = "S13",
  na_item = c("GD", "GD_F3", "GD_F4", "B9", "D41PAY"),
  unit = c("MIO_EUR", "PC_GDP")
))
# gross domestic product at current prices, million euros
gdp <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(geo = "EL", na_item = "B1GQ", unit = "CP_MEUR"))
# one series of the deficit and debt data, by year
series <- function(item, unit, years) {
  s <- edp[edp$na_item == item & edp$unit == unit, ]
  s$values[match(years, s$time)]
}
years <- sort(unique(edp$time[edp$na_item == "GD"]))
greece <- data.frame(
  year = years,
  debt_bn = series("GD", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,          # debt, billion euros
  debt_gdp = series("GD", "PC_GDP", years),                 # debt, % of GDP
  bonds_bn = series("GD_F3", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,      # of which bonds and bills
  loans_bn = series("GD_F4", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,      # of which loans
  balance_gdp = series("B9", "PC_GDP", years),              # surplus (+) or deficit (-), % of GDP
  interest_gdp = series("D41PAY", "PC_GDP", years),         # interest, % of GDP
  interest_bn = series("D41PAY", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,
  gdp_bn = gdp$values[match(years, gdp$time)] / 1000
)
# the balance before interest: what the State collects minus what it spends on everything else
greece$primary_gdp <- greece$balance_gdp + greece$interest_gdp
last <- max(greece$year)
at <- function(column, year) greece[[column]][greece$year == year]
# who holds the debt (from 2020), and when it falls due
holders <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_ggd", list(geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", maturity = "TOTAL", unit = "MIO_EUR"))
due <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_rmd", list(geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = "GD"))
# debt of every EU country, % of GDP, and the countries with the most
eu <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list(sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", unit = "PC_GDP"))
eu_name <- c(setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code), EU27_2020 = "EU-27")
most <- eu[eu$time == last & eu$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ]
most <- most[order(-most$values), ]
# the average years to repayment of the debt of every EU country, the longest first
maturities <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_rmd", list(sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", maturity = "TOTAL", unit = "YR"))
maturities <- maturities[maturities$time == max(maturities$time) & maturities$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ]
maturities <- maturities[order(-maturities$values), ]
# World Bank: interest payments, % of revenue
world_bank <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/GRC/indicator/GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS?format=json&per_page=100")[[2]]
interest_revenue <- data.frame(year = as.integer(world_bank$date), value = world_bank$value)
interest_revenue <- interest_revenue[!is.na(interest_revenue$value), ]
interest_revenue <- interest_revenue[order(interest_revenue$year), ]
Code 
greek_red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left"),
    yaxis = list(title = y_title),
    xaxis = list(title = ""),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
# a short label of an amount
billion <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x), big.mark = ","), " bn")

1. Does Greece owe more now than in 2010?

In euros, yes. As a share of the economy, slightly less — and far less than at the peak.

At the end of 2010 the Greek state owed €331 bn; at the end of 2025 it owed €363 bn, that is €32 bn more. The debt fell only once, in 2012, when private holders of Greek bonds took a loss in the restructuring known as the PSI: between 2011 and 2012 the debt went down by €51 bn, although new bailout loans came in at the same time.

Code 
highlight <- ifelse(greece$year %in% c(2010, last), greek_red, gray)
plot_ly(greece,
  x = ~year, y = ~debt_bn, type = "bar", marker = list(color = highlight),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(
    "Greek government debt, billion euros", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "Billion euros",
    annotations = list(list(
      x = 2012, y = at("debt_bn", 2012), text = "2012: bondholders' haircut (PSI)",
      showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = -60
    ))
  )

Interactive chart: Greek government debt, billion euros

What matters for paying a debt is the size of the economy that carries it. As a share of the gross domestic product (GDP), the debt was 147.8% in 2010 and 145.4% in 2025: about the same. In between it rose to 209.4% in 2020, when the pandemic made the economy shrink, and it has fallen by 64 points since.

Code 
plot_ly(greece,
  x = ~year, y = ~debt_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_lines(x = range(greece$year), y = c(60, 60), line = list(color = gray, dash = "dash"), hoverinfo = "skip", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart(
    "Greek government debt, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "% of GDP",
    showlegend = FALSE,
    annotations = list(
      list(x = greece$year[1], y = 60, text = "60%: the limit of the EU rules", showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom", font = list(color = gray)),
      list(x = greece$year[which.max(greece$debt_gdp)], y = max(greece$debt_gdp), text = "Pandemic", showarrow = TRUE, ax = -50, ay = -30)
    )
  )

Interactive chart: Greek government debt, % of GDP

2. Whom does Greece owe?

Mostly the rest of the euro area, through the rescue funds of the bailouts. In 2010, 79% of the debt was bonds sold to investors; in 2025, 71% is loans. The bailouts replaced most of the bonds with long, cheap loans from the euro area and, until 2022, the IMF.

Code 
plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~bonds_bn, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Bonds and bills",
  line = list(color = gray, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion in bonds<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~loans_bn, name = "Loans", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion in loans<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("From bonds to loans: the debt by instrument, billion euros", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "Billion euros",
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))

Interactive chart: From bonds to loans: the debt by instrument, billion euros

The PDMA names the creditors of the State. At the end of 2025:

Code 
# PDMA, Annual Debt Bulletin 2025 (June 2026), debt of the State at 31.12.2025, million euros (pages 13-14).
# The bulletin gives 211,421 for the loans of the EFSF, the ESM and the GLF together, and says
# that the EFSF and the ESM hold 45.58% of the debt; the GLF is the difference.
total <- 406181
creditors <- data.frame(
  creditor = c(
    "EFSF and ESM: the euro area rescue funds",
    "Bonds held by investors and the Bank of Greece",
    "Repos: short-term loans, mostly from public bodies",
    "GLF: bilateral loans of euro area countries",
    "Other EU and international loans (RRF, SURE, EIB)",
    "Treasury bills"
  ),
  million = c(round(0.4558 * total), 100759, 62852, 211421 - round(0.4558 * total), 23057, 7969)
)
creditors$share <- 100 * creditors$million / total
creditors <- creditors[order(creditors$million), ]
creditors$creditor <- factor(creditors$creditor, levels = creditors$creditor)
plot_ly(creditors,
  x = ~ million / 1000, y = ~creditor, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = c(rep(gray, nrow(creditors) - 1), greek_red)),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share, 1), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: €%{x:.1f} billion<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Who lends to the Greek State, end of 2025, billion euros",
    "PDMA, Annual Debt Bulletin 2025; the GLF as calculated in the code above",
    margin = list(l = 330, r = 60, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Who lends to the Greek State, end of 2025, billion euros

  • The EFSF and the ESM, the rescue funds of the euro area, hold almost half of the debt of the State. Their loans are repaid over decades: those of the EFSF from 2023 to 2070, those of the ESM from 2034 to 2060 (ESM).
  • The GLF loans of the first bailout come from the other euro area countries. Their interest rate floats, so Greece is paying them back early: €5.3 billion in 2025.
  • The IMF was repaid in full in 2022.
  • The repos are mostly the cash of other public bodies, lent to the State for a few days or weeks; the EU measure of the debt leaves them out.

Eurostat’s view of the same debt, by who holds it rather than by instrument:

Code 
groups <- c(
  S2 = "Abroad (the rescue funds, foreign investors)",
  S121 = "Bank of Greece",
  S122_S123 = "Greek banks",
  `S124-S129` = "Other Greek financial companies",
  S11 = "Greek companies",
  S14_S15 = "Greek households"
)
latest_holders <- holders[holders$time == max(holders$time), ]
held <- data.frame(holder = groups, million = latest_holders$values[match(names(groups), latest_holders$sector2)])
held$million[is.na(held$million)] <- 0
held$share <- 100 * held$million / latest_holders$values[latest_holders$sector2 == "S1_S2"]
held <- held[order(held$share), ]
held$holder <- factor(held$holder, levels = held$holder)
plot_ly(held,
  x = ~share, y = ~holder, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(held$holder == groups[["S2"]], greek_red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of the debt<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Who holds the Greek government debt, ", max(holders$time), ", % of the debt"),
    "Eurostat, gov_10dd_ggd", margin = list(l = 300, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Who holds the Greek government debt, 2025, % of the debt

3. How much is it, compared with the economy and with the EU?

At 145.4% of GDP, Greece still has the highest debt in the EU, 8.7 points above Italy.

Code 
eu_latest <- eu[eu$time == last & eu$geo %in% c(eu_countries$code, "EU27_2020"), ]
eu_latest$name <- eu_name[eu_latest$geo]
eu_latest <- eu_latest[order(eu_latest$values), ]
eu_latest$name <- factor(eu_latest$name, levels = eu_latest$name)
plot_ly(eu_latest,
  x = ~values, y = ~name, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(eu_latest$geo == "EL", greek_red, ifelse(eu_latest$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))),
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Government debt in the EU, ", last, ", % of GDP"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1",
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Government debt in the EU, 2025, % of GDP

4. Will Greece be able to repay?

Countries rarely pay their debt off; they repay old loans with new ones. The question is whether the debt stays affordable — whether the interest leaves enough for everything else — and whether it keeps shrinking against the economy. On both, the numbers now look good, for four reasons.

Interest takes far less of the budget

In 2011 interest cost Greece 7.7% of GDP; in 2025, 3.1%. The World Bank’s series shows the same from the side of the budget: interest took 17.8% of the government’s revenue in 2011, and 7.5% in 2024.

Code 
subplot(
  plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~interest_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
    name = "% of GDP (Eurostat)", hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"),
  plot_ly(interest_revenue, x = ~year, y = ~value, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = blue, width = 3),
    name = "% of revenue (World Bank)", hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of revenue<extra></extra>"),
  nrows = 2, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE
) %>%
  chart("Interest paid by the Greek government", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1; World Bank, GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS",
    "% of GDP", yaxis2 = list(title = "% of revenue"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))

Interactive chart: Interest paid by the Greek government

The debt is long, fixed and in euros

Code 
years_left <- due[due$unit == "YR" & due$maturity == "TOTAL", ]
buckets <- c(Y_LE1 = "Up to 1 year", `Y1-5` = "1 to 5 years", `Y5-10` = "5 to 10 years", `Y10-30` = "10 to 30 years", Y_GT30 = "Over 30 years")
falling_due <- due[due$unit == "MIO_EUR" & due$time == max(due$time) & due$maturity %in% names(buckets), ]
falling_due$label <- factor(buckets[falling_due$maturity], levels = buckets)
falling_due$share <- 100 * falling_due$values / sum(falling_due$values)
plot_ly(falling_due,
  x = ~label, y = ~share, type = "bar", marker = list(color = greek_red),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of the debt<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("When the debt falls due, ", max(due$time), ", % of the debt"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_rmd", "% of the debt")

Interactive chart: When the debt falls due, 2025, % of the debt

  • On average the debt falls due in 18.4 years (Eurostat), the longest in the EU: next comes Austria, with 11.3 years.
  • After interest rate swaps, none of it has a floating rate and none is in a foreign currency (PDMA): higher interest rates reach only the debt that is renewed, a little each year.
  • In 2025 the State needed €17.6 billion to repay maturing debt and cover its budget, about 7% of GDP, and borrowed it at 2.89% for 14.6 years on average (PDMA). When the euro area eased the terms of its loans in 2018, it set out to keep these needs below 15% of GDP in the medium term and below 20% after that (Eurogroup, June 2018).
  • The State keeps a cash reserve: the general government held €39.6 billion in cash at the end of 2025, so its debt minus its cash was €323 billion (PDMA).

Why the ratio fell so fast

The change of the debt ratio each year adds up from four parts:

  • Interest adds to the debt.
  • The primary balance (the budget before interest) adds a deficit or takes away a surplus.
  • Growth of the economy in euros — real growth plus inflation — shrinks the ratio, as the same debt is divided by a bigger GDP.
  • Other changes: debt that changes without a deficit, such as the PSI haircut of 2012 or the cash the State borrows ahead and keeps.
Code 
d <- greece[greece$year >= 2010 & !is.na(greece$gdp_bn), ]
n <- nrow(d)
ratio <- 100 * d$debt_bn / d$gdp_bn
growth <- d$gdp_bn[-1] / d$gdp_bn[-n] - 1
parts <- data.frame(
  year = d$year[-1],
  change = diff(ratio),
  interest = 100 * d$interest_bn[-1] / d$gdp_bn[-1],
  primary = -d$primary_gdp[-1],
  growth = -ratio[-n] * growth / (1 + growth)
)
parts$other <- parts$change - parts$interest - parts$primary - parts$growth
plot_ly(parts, x = ~year, y = ~interest, type = "bar", name = "Interest", marker = list(color = greek_red)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~primary, name = "Primary deficit (+) or surplus (-)", marker = list(color = "#ff9896")) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~growth, name = "Growth of GDP in euros", marker = list(color = blue)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~other, name = "Other", marker = list(color = gray)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~change, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", name = "Change of the debt ratio",
    marker = list(color = "black", size = 10, symbol = "diamond")) %>%
  chart("What changed the debt ratio each year, points of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1 and nama_10_gdp; own calculation",
    "Points of GDP", barmode = "relative", note_y = -0.34, margin = list(t = 70, b = 160),
    # under the chart, as its five entries take two lines
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.1, yanchor = "top"))

Interactive chart: What changed the debt ratio each year, points of GDP

From 2021 the economy grew fast in euros — partly real growth, partly inflation — while the interest rate on the debt stayed low: growth alone took 71 points off the ratio between 2021 and 2025. The budget before interest was in deficit in the pandemic and then turned to surplus: from 2023, the surpluses took 12 points more.

Where it could go: three scenarios

The debt ratio of next year is this year’s, grown by the interest rate and shrunk by the growth of GDP in euros, minus the primary surplus:

\[d_{t} = d_{t-1} \times \frac{1 + i_t}{1 + g_t} - pb_t\]

The scenarios below start from the 2025 debt and its average interest rate of 2.1%, which climbs over ten years as cheap loans are replaced by new borrowing at market rates. They are illustrations of what drives the debt, not forecasts.

Code 
start_rate <- at("interest_bn", last) / at("debt_bn", last - 1)
assumptions <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Strong", "Steady", "Weak"),
  growth = c(0.050, 0.040, 0.025),    # growth of GDP in euros, a year
  rate_to = c(0.025, 0.030, 0.040),   # average interest rate on the debt after ten years
  primary = c(3.5, 2.5, 1.0)          # primary surplus, % of GDP
)
project <- function(growth, rate_to, primary, years = (last + 1):2040) {
  debt <- at("debt_gdp", last)
  path <- numeric(length(years))
  for (k in seq_along(years)) {
    rate <- start_rate + (rate_to - start_rate) * min(1, k / 10)
    debt <- debt * (1 + rate) / (1 + growth) - primary
    path[k] <- debt
  }
  data.frame(year = c(last, years), debt_gdp = c(at("debt_gdp", last), path))
}
paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(assumptions)), function(k) {
  cbind(scenario = assumptions$scenario[k], project(assumptions$growth[k], assumptions$rate_to[k], assumptions$primary[k]))
}))
in_2040 <- setNames(paths$debt_gdp[paths$year == 2040], paths$scenario[paths$year == 2040])
knitr::kable(transform(assumptions,
  growth = paste0(100 * growth, "%"), rate_to = paste0(100 * rate_to, "%"), primary = paste0(primary, "% of GDP"),
  debt_2040 = paste0(round(in_2040[scenario]), "% of GDP")
), col.names = c("Scenario", "GDP growth in euros, a year", "Interest rate after ten years", "Primary surplus", "Debt in 2040"))
Scenario GDP growth in euros, a year Interest rate after ten years Primary surplus Debt in 2040
Strong 5% 2.5% 3.5% of GDP 55% of GDP
Steady 4% 3% 2.5% of GDP 86% of GDP
Weak 2.5% 4% 1% of GDP 150% of GDP
Code 
plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~debt_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Actual",
  line = list(color = "black", width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Strong", ], name = "Strong", line = list(color = blue, dash = "dot")) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Steady", ], name = "Steady", line = list(color = greek_red, dash = "dot")) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Weak", ], name = "Weak", line = list(color = gray, dash = "dot")) %>%
  chart("Greek government debt to 2040: three scenarios, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1; own scenarios", "% of GDP",
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))

Interactive chart: Greek government debt to 2040: three scenarios, % of GDP

In the steady scenario the debt falls to about 86% of GDP by 2040. In the weak one it ends near 150%, a little above today’s level: with long, fixed and cheap loans, a bad decade would stop the fall rather than send the debt back to the heights of 2020.

So, will Greece repay?

On today’s numbers, yes: the debt is large, but it is cheap, it falls due slowly, and it is shrinking against the economy. The markets agree: Greece is back in the investment grade (Moody’s raised it to Baa3 in March 2025), and at the end of 2025 its ten-year bonds paid only 0.59 percentage points more than Germany’s (PDMA).

What could still go wrong:

  • A recession, or years of slow growth: growth did most of the work since 2021.
  • Higher interest rates on the debt that is renewed each year, and more of it once the cheap rescue loans start falling due in the 2030s.
  • Smaller surpluses: the scenarios need primary surpluses for many years, which is a political choice, not only an economic one.
  • An ageing population, which raises the cost of pensions and health care.

Sources

  • Eurostat: gov_10dd_edpt1 (deficit, debt and interest), gov_10dd_ggd (holders of the debt), gov_10dd_rmd (remaining maturity), nama_10_gdp (GDP).
  • World Bank: Interest payments (% of revenue), GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS.
  • PDMA, Ministry of Finance: Annual Debt Bulletin 2025 (in Greek, June 2026).
  • ESM: When will Greece repay ESM and EFSF loans?

See also

  • golemworldbank: an interactive explorer of the World Bank development indicators of every country (open the app)
