item.title: Tobit Regression: A Worked Example
item.description: Tobit regression for an outcome censored at zero, fitted in R with AER and censReg on simulated data, explained step by step and reported in APA style.
item.content:encoded:
Tobit regression for an outcome censored at zero, fitted in R with AER and censReg on simulated data, explained step by step and reported in APA style.

The problem: a pile of zeros

Imagine we ask 500 people how many hours per week they spend on sport. Many answer 0. Not because they all have exactly the same “zero” interest in sport: some are almost ready to start, others would never do it. We only see 0, because hours cannot go below 0.

This is called a censored outcome: below a limit (here 0) we do not see the true value, only the limit itself.

A Tobit model assumes there is an unobserved (latent) variable \(y^*\), the person’s “desire” for sport, that follows an ordinary linear regression:

\[y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]

and what we observe is

\[y = \begin{cases} y^* & \text{if } y^* > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } y^* \le 0 \end{cases}\]

To see why we need it, we simulate data where we know the true answer, and compare three methods.

Code 
library(survival)   # survreg(): fits the Tobit model (comes with R)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side

1. Simulate the data

The true model: every extra hour of free time per day adds 2 hours of sport per week (\(\beta_1 = 2\)), starting from \(-4\) (\(\beta_0 = -4\)), with noise \(\sigma = 3\).

Code 
set.seed(42)
n <- 500
free_time <- runif(n, 0, 6)                         # hours of free time per day
latent    <- -4 + 2 * free_time + rnorm(n, sd = 3)  # y*: the true "desire" (can be negative)
hours     <- pmax(latent, 0)                        # y: what we observe (never below 0)
df <- data.frame(free_time, latent, hours, censored = latent <= 0)
mean(df$censored)   # share of people we see as 0
[1] 0.362

About a third of the people are recorded as exactly 0.

2. Look at the data

Code 
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "What we observe", x = "hours of sport per week", y = "people")
p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(latent, fill = censored)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#0082c8", `TRUE` = "#E74C3C"),
                    labels = c("observed", "hidden: recorded as 0")) +
  labs(title = "The truth (never seen in real life)", x = "latent y*", y = "people", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p1 + p2

Left: the big bar at 0 is the pile-up. Right: behind that bar are many different negative values (red), all squeezed into a single 0.

Code 
ggplot(df, aes(free_time)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = latent), colour = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = hours), colour = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Red: the true y*.  Blue: what we observe (red points below 0 are moved up to 0)",
       x = "free time (hours per day)", y = "hours of sport")

3. Three ways to fit it

Code 
ols_all  <- lm(hours ~ free_time, data = df)                    # (a) ignore the problem
ols_pos  <- lm(hours ~ free_time, data = subset(df, hours > 0)) # (b) drop the zeros
tobit    <- survreg(Surv(hours, hours > 0, type = "left") ~ free_time,
                    data = df, dist = "gaussian")               # (c) Tobit
summary(tobit)

Call:
survreg(formula = Surv(hours, hours > 0, type = "left") ~ free_time, 
    data = df, dist = "gaussian")
              Value Std. Error     z      p
(Intercept) -4.0633     0.3514 -11.6 <2e-16
free_time    1.9795     0.0923  21.4 <2e-16
Log(scale)   1.0818     0.0410  26.4 <2e-16
Scale= 2.95 
Gaussian distribution
Loglik(model)= -896.3   Loglik(intercept only)= -1095.5
    Chisq= 398.29 on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 1.3e-88 
Number of Newton-Raphson Iterations: 6 
n= 500

Surv(hours, hours > 0, type = "left") tells R: “hours is the value, it is a real observation when hours > 0, and otherwise it is left-censored (the true value is somewhere at or below 0).” With dist = "gaussian" this is exactly the Tobit model. (AER::tobit(hours ~ free_time, left = 0) gives the same result with a shorter call.)

How to read the output

The output of summary(tobit) above, part by part. The coefficient table is also available as numbers, which we use below:

Code 
s <- summary(tobit)$table   # Value, Std. Error, z, p for each row
signif(s, 4)                # signif, not round: round() would print the tiny p values as 0
             Value Std. Error      z          p
(Intercept) -4.063    0.35140 -11.56  6.249e-31
free_time    1.980    0.09227  21.45 4.135e-102
Log(scale)   1.082    0.04101  26.38 2.418e-153

The coefficient table. Each row is one parameter:

Column Meaning Here, for free_time
Value The estimate \(b\): the change in the latent \(y^*\) for one unit more of the predictor 1.98: one more hour of free time per day raises the latent amount of sport by about 2 hours per week
Std. Error How uncertain the estimate is; smaller is more precise 0.09
z Value / Std. Error: how many standard errors the estimate is away from 0 1.9795 / 0.0923 = 21.45
p The chance of a z this large if the true effect were 0. <2e-16 means smaller than 0.0000000000000002: report it as p < .001 <2e-16
  • (Intercept) (-4.06) is the predicted latent value for someone with 0 hours of free time. It is below 0, which means such a person is predicted to do no sport at all. It is not a prediction of observed hours, which can never be negative.
  • Log(scale) is the logarithm of \(\sigma\), the standard deviation of the errors. Its z and p test whether \(\sigma = 1\), which is not an interesting question: ignore them.
  • Scale= is \(\sigma\) itself (2.95; the true value in our simulation is 3). It is the spread of \(y^*\) around the regression line, and it is needed for the formulas in section 4.
  • Gaussian distribution confirms that the errors are assumed normal, which is what makes this a Tobit model.
  • Loglik(model) and Loglik(intercept only) measure how well the model with and without free_time fits the data (higher, i.e. closer to 0, is better).
  • Chisq= ... on 1 degrees of freedom, p= ... is the likelihood-ratio test: twice the difference of the two log-likelihoods, \(2 \times (-896.3 - (-1095.5)) = 398.29\). It tests whether the predictors together improve the model; the degrees of freedom are the number of predictors.
  • Number of Newton-Raphson Iterations is technical: the estimation converged after that many steps. If R warns that it did not converge, do not trust the results.
  • n= counts all participants, the censored ones too: Tobit uses them, which is the whole point.

Two things are not in the output. There is no \(R^2\): Tobit is fitted by maximum likelihood, so use the likelihood-ratio test to judge the model. And the coefficients are effects on the latent \(y^*\), not on the observed hours; for those, see sections 4 and 5.

Code 
data.frame(
  method    = c("Truth", "(a) OLS, all data", "(b) OLS, zeros dropped", "(c) Tobit"),
  intercept = round(c(-4, coef(ols_all)[1], coef(ols_pos)[1], coef(tobit)[1]), 2),
  slope     = round(c( 2, coef(ols_all)[2], coef(ols_pos)[2], coef(tobit)[2]), 2)
)
                  method intercept slope
1                  Truth     -4.00  2.00
2      (a) OLS, all data     -1.09  1.34
3 (b) OLS, zeros dropped     -0.28  1.26
4              (c) Tobit     -4.06  1.98
Code 
grid <- data.frame(free_time = seq(0, 6, length.out = 100))
lines <- rbind(
  data.frame(grid, y = -4 + 2 * grid$free_time,         method = "Truth"),
  data.frame(grid, y = predict(ols_all, grid),          method = "(a) OLS, all data"),
  data.frame(grid, y = predict(ols_pos, grid),          method = "(b) OLS, zeros dropped"),
  data.frame(grid, y = predict(tobit, grid),            method = "(c) Tobit")
)
ggplot(df, aes(free_time, hours)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = lines, aes(y = y, colour = method, linetype = method), linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Truth" = "black", "(a) OLS, all data" = "#E74C3C",
                                 "(b) OLS, zeros dropped" = "#f39c12", "(c) Tobit" = "#0082c8")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Truth" = "dashed", "(a) OLS, all data" = "solid",
                                   "(b) OLS, zeros dropped" = "solid", "(c) Tobit" = "solid")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Only Tobit recovers the true line", x = "free time (hours per day)",
       y = "hours of sport", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
  • (a) OLS on all data is too flat: the zeros pull the left end of the line up, so the effect of free time looks smaller than it is.
  • (b) OLS without the zeros is also too flat: we kept only people whose noise happened to be high enough, so the sample is no longer random.
  • (c) Tobit lands on the true line, because it uses the zeros correctly: as “somewhere at or below 0”, not as “exactly 0”.

4. The model step by step, with formulas

Two functions of the normal (bell) curve appear in every formula below:

  • \(\phi(z)\) (“small phi”) is the height of the standard normal curve at \(z\). In R: dnorm(z).
  • \(\Phi(z)\) (“capital phi”) is the area under the curve to the left of \(z\): the share of a normal population that lies below \(z\) standard deviations. In R: pnorm(z). For example \(\Phi(0) = 0.5\) and \(\Phi(1.96) = 0.975\).

Step 1: a straight line (yes, \(y = ax + b\))

At its heart, the Tobit model is the straight line from school, \(y = ax + b\). Statistics books write it as

\[y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]

  • \(\beta_1\) is the \(a\): the slope, how much the line goes up for one unit more of \(x\).
  • \(\beta_0\) is the \(b\): the intercept, the height of the line at \(x = 0\).
Code 
b0 <- unname(coef(tobit)["(Intercept)"])   # the "b" of y = ax + b
b1 <- unname(coef(tobit)["free_time"])     # the "a": the slope
sigma <- tobit$scale
x0 <- 3                                     # a person with 3 hours of free time per day
line0 <- b0 + b1 * x0
line0
[1] 1.875369

For a person with \(x = 3\) hours of free time:

\[y^* = -4.06 + 1.98 \times 3 = 1.88\]

What makes Tobit different from ordinary regression is steps 2 and 3.

Step 2: people are scattered around the line

\[y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]

Two people with the same free time do not want the same amount of sport. \(\varepsilon\) (“epsilon”) is how far each person is from the line. It is normally distributed around 0 with standard deviation \(\sigma\) = 2.95, so about two thirds of the people are within \(\pm\) 2.95 hours of the line, and about 95% within \(\pm 2\sigma\).

Step 3: the floor at 0

\[y = \max(0,\; y^*)\]

We see \(y^*\) only when it is positive. Everyone whose \(y^*\) falls at or below 0 is recorded as exactly 0.

Step 4: the chance of being at 0

For a person with free time \(x\), the line is at \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) and \(y^*\) is spread around it with standard deviation \(\sigma\). The chance of falling at or below 0 is the area of that bell curve below 0:

\[P(y = 0 \mid x) = P(y^* \le 0) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{0 - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}{\sigma}\right)\]

In words: how many standard deviations is 0 below the line, and what share of the bell curve lies below that point? Writing \(z = \frac{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}{\sigma}\) for the height of the line in standard deviations, this is \(\Phi(-z)\), and the chance of doing some sport is \(P(y > 0 \mid x) = \Phi(z)\).

Code 
z0 <- line0 / sigma                 # the line at x = 3, in standard deviations
p_zero <- pnorm(-z0)                # Φ(-z): the area of the bell curve below 0
c(z = z0, chance_of_zero = p_zero)
             z chance_of_zero 
     0.6357350      0.2624746
Code 
near <- abs(df$free_time - x0) < 0.5       # people in the data with 2.5 to 3.5 hours
mean(df$hours[near] == 0)                   # the share of them who are at 0: close to the formula
[1] 0.2282609

For \(x = 3\): \(z = 1.88 / 2.95 = 0.64\), so \(P(y = 0) = \Phi(-0.64) = 0.26\): about 26% of such people do no sport.

Code 
dens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 3, 5), function(x) {
  mu <- b0 + b1 * x
  y <- seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 400)
  data.frame(y = y, d = dnorm(y, mu, sigma),
             label = sprintf("free time = %d hour%s: line at %.2f, P(y = 0) = %.2f",
                             x, ifelse(x == 1, "", "s"), mu, pnorm(-mu / sigma)))
}))
ggplot(dens, aes(y, d)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(dens, y <= 0), fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~label, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Where y* can fall for three people. The red area is recorded as 0",
       x = "latent y* (hours of sport per week)", y = "density")

The more free time, the further the bell curve moves to the right, and the smaller the red area.

Step 5: how R finds \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma\)

R uses maximum likelihood: it looks for the values that make the data we saw as likely as possible. Every person adds one piece:

  • A person with \(y_i > 0\): we know the exact value, so the piece is the height of their bell curve at that value: \(\frac{1}{\sigma}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)}{\sigma}\right)\), in R dnorm(y, mean = line, sd = sigma).
  • A person with \(y_i = 0\): we only know that \(y^* \le 0\), so the piece is the red area of their bell curve: \(\Phi\!\left(\frac{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)}{\sigma}\right)\), in R pnorm(-line / sigma).

Adding the logarithms of all the pieces gives the log-likelihood:

\[\log L = \sum_{y_i > 0} \log\!\left[\frac{1}{\sigma}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i}{\sigma}\right)\right] + \sum_{y_i = 0} \log \Phi\!\left(\frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i}{\sigma}\right)\]

R tries values of \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma\) until \(\log L\) is as large as possible. With the estimates, our hand calculation gives exactly the Loglik(model) of the output:

Code 
line_i <- b0 + b1 * df$free_time      # the line for every person
pos    <- df$hours > 0
loglik_by_hand <- sum(log(dnorm(df$hours[pos], mean = line_i[pos], sd = sigma))) +   # people above 0: heights
                  sum(log(pnorm(-line_i[!pos] / sigma)))                             # people at 0: areas
c(by_hand = loglik_by_hand, from_R = tobit$loglik[2])
  by_hand    from_R 
-896.3469 -896.3469

Ordinary regression (OLS) instead treats every 0 as an exact value of 0, the first kind of piece, which is why its line comes out too flat.

Step 6: three different “averages”

For people with free time \(x\), with \(z = \frac{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}{\sigma}\) as before, there are three different average amounts of sport:

  1. The line, the average of \(y^*\) (it can be negative): \(E[y^* \mid x] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)
  2. Among the people who do some sport: \(E[y \mid y > 0, x] = (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) + \sigma \, \dfrac{\phi(z)}{\Phi(z)}\). It is above the line, because the people with the lowest \(y^*\) have dropped out to 0.
  3. Among everybody, zeros included: \(E[y \mid x] = \Phi(z)\,(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) + \sigma\,\phi(z)\). This is the chance of doing any sport times the average of those who do: \(P(y > 0) \times E[y \mid y > 0]\).
Code 
e_line      <- line0
e_positive  <- line0 + sigma * dnorm(z0) / pnorm(z0)
e_everybody <- pnorm(z0) * line0 + sigma * dnorm(z0)
round(c(line = e_line, among_those_doing_sport = e_positive, everybody = e_everybody), 2)
                   line among_those_doing_sport               everybody 
                   1.88                    3.18                    2.34
Code 
# the same in the data, for people with 2.5 to 3.5 hours of free time
round(c(among_those_doing_sport = mean(df$hours[near & df$hours > 0]), everybody = mean(df$hours[near])), 2)
among_those_doing_sport               everybody 
                   3.05                    2.36
Code 
x  <- seq(0, 6, length.out = 200)
zx <- (b0 + b1 * x) / sigma
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(free_time = x, y = b0 + b1 * x, what = "1. the line, E[y*]"),
  data.frame(free_time = x, y = b0 + b1 * x + sigma * dnorm(zx) / pnorm(zx), what = "2. those doing sport, E[y | y > 0]"),
  data.frame(free_time = x, y = pnorm(zx) * (b0 + b1 * x) + sigma * dnorm(zx), what = "3. everybody, E[y]"))
ggplot(df, aes(free_time, hours)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(y = y, colour = what, linetype = what), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "#f39c12", "#0082c8")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid", "solid")) +
  labs(title = "Three averages: they come together when almost nobody is at 0",
       x = "free time (hours per day)", y = "hours of sport per week", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Step 7: the effect of one more unit of \(x\)

The effect is the slope of each “average” from step 6:

  • On the latent \(y^*\), the slope of the straight line: \(\dfrac{\partial E[y^*]}{\partial x} = \beta_1\)
  • On the observed hours, the slope times the chance of being above 0: \(\dfrac{\partial E[y \mid x]}{\partial x} = \beta_1\,\Phi(z)\)
  • On the chance of doing any sport: \(\dfrac{\partial P(y > 0 \mid x)}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\beta_1}{\sigma}\,\phi(z)\)

The average marginal effect is the second one, averaged over all \(n\) people: \(\text{AME} = \beta_1 \cdot \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \Phi(z_i)\).

Code 
me_line  <- b1                                   # effect on y*
me_hours <- b1 * pnorm(z0)                       # effect on the observed hours, at x = 3
me_prob  <- b1 / sigma * dnorm(z0)               # effect on the chance of doing any sport, at x = 3
ame_hand <- b1 * mean(pnorm(line_i / sigma))     # effect on the observed hours, averaged over everybody
round(c(on_y_star = me_line, on_hours_at_3 = me_hours, on_chance_at_3 = me_prob, average_on_hours = ame_hand), 3)
       on_y_star    on_hours_at_3   on_chance_at_3 average_on_hours 
           1.980            1.460            0.219            1.257

For a person with 3 hours of free time, one more hour adds \(1.98 \times 0.74 = 1.46\) hours of sport and raises the chance of doing any sport by about 22 percentage points. Averaged over everybody, it adds 1.26 hours: the same number as in section 5.

All the formulas at once

Quantity Formula R
The line (the \(ax + b\)) \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) b0 + b1 * x
The line in standard deviations \(z = (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) / \sigma\) z <- (b0 + b1 * x) / sigma
Chance of being at 0 \(\Phi(-z)\) pnorm(-z)
Chance of being above 0 \(\Phi(z)\) pnorm(z)
Average among those above 0 \((\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) + \sigma\,\phi(z) / \Phi(z)\) b0 + b1 * x + sigma * dnorm(z) / pnorm(z)
Average among everybody \(\Phi(z)(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) + \sigma\,\phi(z)\) pnorm(z) * (b0 + b1 * x) + sigma * dnorm(z)
Effect on \(y^*\) \(\beta_1\) b1
Effect on the observed \(y\) \(\beta_1\,\Phi(z)\) b1 * pnorm(z)
Effect on the chance of being above 0 \(\beta_1\,\phi(z) / \sigma\) b1 / sigma * dnorm(z)

5. Interpreting the coefficients

The Tobit slope (1.98) is the effect on the latent \(y^*\): one more hour of free time raises the desire for sport by about 2 hours. But often we want the effect on what we actually see. Two useful quantities (here \(X\beta\) is short for the line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) of section 4):

  1. Probability of doing any sport: \(P(y > 0) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{X\beta}{\sigma}\right)\)
  2. Expected observed hours: \(E[y] = \Phi\!\left(\frac{X\beta}{\sigma}\right) X\beta + \sigma\, \phi\!\left(\frac{X\beta}{\sigma}\right)\)
Code 
sigma <- tobit$scale
xb    <- predict(tobit, grid)              # X * beta, the latent prediction
grid$p_any  <- pnorm(xb / sigma)
grid$e_hours <- pnorm(xb / sigma) * xb + sigma * dnorm(xb / sigma)
p3 <- ggplot(grid, aes(free_time, p_any)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Chance of doing any sport", x = "free time (hours per day)", y = NULL)
p4 <- ggplot(df, aes(free_time, hours)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = e_hours), colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(title = "Expected observed hours (a curve!)", x = "free time (hours per day)", y = "hours")
p3 + p4

The expected observed hours is a curve, flat near 0 (most people do nothing anyway) and close to the latent line for people with lots of free time. So the effect of one more hour of free time depends on where you are:

Code 
# average marginal effect on the observed hours: beta * P(y > 0), averaged over the people in the data
xb_people <- predict(tobit, df)
ame <- unname(coef(tobit)["free_time"]) * mean(pnorm(xb_people / sigma))
round(c(latent_effect = unname(coef(tobit)["free_time"]), effect_on_observed_hours = ame), 2)
           latent_effect effect_on_observed_hours 
                    1.98                     1.26

On average, one more hour of free time adds about 1.26 hours of observed sport, less than the latent effect, because for some people it is not enough to start doing sport at all.

Checking it with a package

The censReg package fits the same Tobit model and computes marginal effects for us (install.packages("censReg")):

Code 
library(censReg)
m <- censReg(hours ~ free_time, left = 0, data = df)
coef(m)   # same intercept and slope as survreg; logSigma is log(sigma)
(Intercept)   free_time    logSigma 
  -4.063264    1.979544    1.081779

margEff() gives the effect on the observed hours. Careful: by default it is the effect for a person with average free time (2.9 hours), not the average over all people:

Code 
summary(margEff(m))   # effect at the average free time
          Marg. Eff. Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)    
free_time   1.432509   0.065628  21.828 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Read this like the coefficient table: Marg. Eff. is the effect on the observed hours, Std. Error its uncertainty, and t value and Pr(>|t|) test whether it differs from 0.

To get the average marginal effect, compute the effect for each person and take the mean. It matches the value we calculated by hand above:

Code 
each_person <- sapply(df$free_time, function(x) margEff(m, xValues = c(1, x)))   # 1 = the intercept
round(c(at_average_person = unname(margEff(m)), average_over_people = mean(each_person), by_hand = ame), 2)
  at_average_person average_over_people             by_hand 
               1.43                1.26                1.26

The two differ because the effect is not the same for everyone: it is small for people with little free time (most of them do no sport anyway) and close to 1.98 for people with a lot. The effect at the average person is not the average of the effects.

6. Reporting the results in APA style

A psychology report (APA 7th edition) needs the reason for using Tobit, the estimates with their uncertainty, the model test, and what the effect means on the observed scale. We collect the numbers from the R objects, so the text below always matches the results:

Code 
n       <- nrow(df)
n_cens  <- sum(df$hours == 0)                                  # participants at the limit
se      <- s[, "Std. Error"]
ci_low  <- s[, "Value"] - qnorm(0.975) * se                     # 95% confidence interval
ci_high <- s[, "Value"] + qnorm(0.975) * se
lr      <- 2 * diff(tobit$loglik)                               # likelihood-ratio test
lr_p    <- pchisq(lr, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
mem     <- summary(margEff(m))                                  # effect at the average person
# APA number formats: 2 decimals, p without a leading zero, "< .001" for tiny p
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))

Method (data analysis):

Because 181 of the 500 participants (36.2%) reported no sport at all, weekly hours of sport were left-censored at zero. We therefore analysed them with a Tobit (censored) regression, which treats these zeros as values at or below the censoring point rather than as true zeros. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the survival and censReg packages.

Results:

More daily free time predicted more weekly sport, b = 1.98, SE = 0.09, z = 21.45, p < .001, 95% CI [1.80, 2.16], and the model fitted the data better than an intercept-only model, χ²(1) = 398.29, p < .001. The coefficient refers to the latent (uncensored) amount of sport: each additional hour of free time per day was associated with about 2 more hours of sport per week. On the observed scale, the average marginal effect was 1.26: averaged across participants, one more hour of free time per day was associated with 1.26 more hours of sport per week. For a participant with average free time (M = 2.94 hours), the effect was 1.43, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [1.30, 1.56].

Table 1

Tobit Regression Predicting Weekly Hours of Sport From Daily Free Time

Predictor b SE z p 95% CI
Intercept -4.06 0.35 -11.56 < .001 [-4.75, -3.37]
Free time (hours/day) 1.98 0.09 21.45 < .001 [1.80, 2.16]

Note. N = 500; 181 observations (36.2%) were left-censored at 0. σ = 2.95. Likelihood-ratio test against the intercept-only model: χ²(1) = 398.29, p < .001. Coefficients are effects on the latent outcome.

Points to remember:

  • Put statistical symbols in italics (b, SE, z, p, M); write p without a leading zero, and p < .001 for anything smaller.
  • Say why you used Tobit: how many values sit at the limit.
  • Say what the coefficient means: an effect on the latent variable.
  • Say which marginal effect you report: the average over participants, or the effect at the average participant. They differ (here 1.26 and 1.43).
  • Give 95% confidence intervals. The interval of the average marginal effect is not in the R output; get it with a bootstrap, or report only the effect at the average participant, which has an SE.
  • Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("survival") in R give the exact references.

7. Summary

When The outcome has a pile-up at a limit (0, a maximum score, a detection limit) because values beyond it cannot be recorded
Why not OLS It treats the pile-up as real values and gives a biased, usually too flat, slope
Why not drop the zeros The remaining sample is selected, which also biases the slope
How (R) survreg(Surv(y, y > lower, type = "left") ~ x, dist = "gaussian") or AER::tobit(y ~ x, left = 0)
Interpretation Coefficients are effects on the latent \(y^*\); compute marginal effects for the observed \(y\) (censReg::margEff()), and say whether it is at the average person or averaged over people
Assumptions Normal errors with constant variance; one process decides both whether and how much
If the last assumption fails e.g. people decide separately whether to do sport and how much: use a two-part (hurdle) model

References

Amemiya, T. (1984). Tobit models: A survey. Journal of Econometrics, 24(1–2), 3–61.

Henningsen, A. (2026). censReg: Censored regression (Tobit) models (R package version 0.5-40). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=censReg

McDonald, J. F., & Moffitt, R. A. (1980). The uses of Tobit analysis. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 62(2), 318–321.

Therneau, T. (2026). A package for survival analysis in R (R package version 3.8-12). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=survival

Tobin, J. (1958). Estimation of relationships for limited dependent variables. Econometrica, 26(1), 24–36.

item.title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
item.description: Fertility below the 2.1 replacement rate and population ageing since 1960 in World Bank data, with world maps, country trends and population pyramids in R.
item.content:encoded:
Fertility below the 2.1 replacement rate and population ageing since 1960 in World Bank data, with world maps, country trends and population pyramids in R.

What is this?

For a population to stay the same size, without people moving in or out, women need to have about 2.1 children each: two to replace the parents, and a little more because some children die young and slightly more boys than girls are born. In 1960 almost every country in the world was far above that. Today more than half of all countries are below it, and some are far below: in South Korea women have fewer than one child each.

This data story shows, in plain words:

  • how many countries have dropped below 2.1, year by year since 1960,
  • where — a world map that changes year by year,
  • how fast — the path of ten countries, from Niger to South Korea, with Greece in red,
  • what it does to a country — population pyramids that turn upside down as fewer children are born and people live longer.

All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators; the page carries its own copy of the data it needs, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "plotly"))
# The data comes from golemworldbank, copied next to this page in R/mfi_fertility.rds.
# For every country and indicator, install golemworldbank itself; its data is in
# Git LFS, so install it from a clone (install_github() can download LFS pointer
# files instead of the data):
#   git lfs install
#   git clone https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank.git
# then in R:
#   devtools::install_local("golemworldbank")
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)          # interactive charts

The data

golemworldbank ships the World Bank’s World Development Indicators as one long table, mfi: one row per country, indicator and year. R/mfi_fertility.rds holds four of its indicators for every country, and the age of the population for six countries:

Code 
# part of golemworldbank's mfi (with the package installed, its mfi has every indicator)
mfi <- readRDS(paste0(directory, "R/mfi_fertility.rds"))
indicators <- c(
  fertility  = "Fertility rate, total (births per woman)",
  aged_65    = "Population ages 65 and above (% of total population)",
  children   = "Population ages 0-14 (% of total population)",
  population = "Population, total"
)
df_world <- mfi %>%
  filter(`Indicator Name` %in% indicators) %>%
  mutate(country = recode(`Country Name`, "Korea, Rep." = "South Korea"),
         code    = `Country Code`,
         year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         measure = names(indicators)[match(`Indicator Name`, indicators)]) %>%
  select(country, code, measure, year, value) %>%
  arrange(country, measure, year)
# the population pyramids: the share of men, and of women, in each five-year age group
ages <- c(sprintf("%02d-%02d", seq(0, 75, 5), seq(4, 79, 5)), "80 and above")
df_ages <- mfi %>%
  filter(grepl("^Population ages .*, (male|female) \\(% of (male|female) population\\)$", `Indicator Name`)) %>%
  mutate(country = recode(`Country Name`, "Korea, Rep." = "South Korea"),
         year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         sex     = ifelse(grepl(", female", `Indicator Name`), "Women", "Men"),
         age     = sub("^Population ages (.*), (male|female).*$", "\\1", `Indicator Name`)) %>%
  filter(age %in% ages) %>%
  mutate(age = factor(sub("80 and above", "80+", age), levels = sub("80 and above", "80+", ages))) %>%
  select(country, year, sex, age, value)
head(df_world, 12)
       country code measure year    value
1  Afghanistan  AFG aged_65 1960 2.823362
2  Afghanistan  AFG aged_65 1961 2.809357
3  Afghanistan  AFG aged_65 1962 2.792835
4  Afghanistan  AFG aged_65 1963 2.775057

Column Description
country Country name (World Bank names, except “South Korea” for “Korea, Rep.”)
code Three-letter country code, for the map
measure fertility children per woman, aged_65 and children the share of people aged 65 and over and under 15, population the number of people
year Year of observation
value The World Bank’s value for that country and year

The fertility rate is the number of children a woman would have over her life if, at each age, she had children at the rate women of that age had them that year. It describes one year, not one family: a rate of 1.5 means that at that year’s pace, ten women would have fifteen children between them.

Code 
replacement <- 2.1   # children per woman that keep a population steady
last_year <- max(df_world$year[df_world$measure == "fertility"])
at <- function(m, cty, y) df_world$value[df_world$measure == m & df_world$country == cty & df_world$year == y]
# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}
# data source as a footnote inside each chart, at the bottom of the bottom
# margin `b` (in pixels), so it lands in the same place whatever the height
source_note <- function(b) {
  list(text = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, via <a href='https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank'>golemworldbank</a>",
       xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
       xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
       font = list(size = 11, color = "gray50"))
}
# end labels: each sits right of its line's last point. Labels closer than
# `gap` pixels are pushed apart, each group of crowded labels centred on its
# lines, and joined to their point by a leader line. `per_px` is how many y
# units one pixel of the plot is worth
end_labels <- function(ends, per_px, highlight = "", gap = 17) {
  o <- order(ends$value)
  y <- ends$value[o]
  step <- gap * per_px
  for (pass in 1:3) {
    for (i in seq_along(y)[-1]) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + step)
    group <- cumsum(c(TRUE, diff(y) > step + 1e-9))
    y <- y - ave(y - ends$value[o], group)            # centre each group on its lines
  }
  for (i in seq_along(y)[-1]) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + step)
  ends$label_y[o] <- y
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(ends)), function(i) {
    name <- if (ends$country[i] == highlight) paste0("<b>", ends$country[i], "</b>") else ends$country[i]
    list(x = ends$year[i], y = ends$value[i], xref = "x", yref = "y",
         ax = 24, ay = -(ends$label_y[i] - ends$value[i]) / per_px,
         showarrow = TRUE, arrowhead = 0, arrowwidth = 1, arrowcolor = "#B3B3B3",
         xanchor = "left", text = paste0(name, " ", ends$text[i]),
         font = list(size = 12, color = "gray25"))
  })
}
# the dotted 2.1 line
replacement_line <- list(type = "line", xref = "paper", x0 = 0, x1 = 1, y0 = replacement, y1 = replacement,
                         line = list(dash = "dot", color = "gray"))

More than half the world is below 2.1

Code 
counts <- df_world %>%
  filter(measure %in% c("fertility", "aged_65", "children")) %>%
  select(-code) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(countries     = sum(!is.na(fertility)),
            low_fertility = sum(fertility < replacement, na.rm = TRUE),
            more_old      = sum(aged_65 > children, na.rm = TRUE),
            median        = median(fertility, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(year <= last_year)
first <- counts[counts$year == min(counts$year), ]
latest <- counts[counts$year == last_year, ]
h <- 520; b <- 150
p <- plot_ly(counts, x = ~year) %>%
  add_lines(y = ~low_fertility, name = "Women have fewer than 2.1 children",
            line = list(color = "#0082c8", width = 3),
            text = ~paste0(year, ": ", low_fertility, " of ", countries, " countries"), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
  add_lines(y = ~more_old, name = "More people over 65 than under 15",
            line = list(color = "#E74C3C", width = 3),
            text = ~paste0(year, ": ", more_old, " countries"), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title  = list(text = "Number of countries where...", x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(t = 80, r = 60, b = b),
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, dtick = 5),
    yaxis  = list(title = "countries", rangemode = "tozero"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
    annotations = list(
      list(x = last_year, y = latest$low_fertility, xanchor = "left", xshift = 6, showarrow = FALSE,
           text = latest$low_fertility, font = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")),
      list(x = last_year, y = latest$more_old, xanchor = "left", xshift = 6, showarrow = FALSE,
           text = latest$more_old, font = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")),
      source_note(b)),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25"))
sized(p, h)

Interactive chart: Number of countries where...

In 1960, women had fewer than 2.1 children in just 5 of 216 countries. By 2024 it was 119 of 217 — more than half. In the middle country of the world, the number of children per woman fell from 6.1 to 1.9.

Fewer children, and people living longer, change the shape of a country. In 1960 there was 1 country with more people over 65 than children under 15; in 2024 there were 53. The red line follows the blue one about 35 years later — 20 countries in 1972 and 2006, 50 in 1987 and 2024: the children who are not born today are the working-age people who will be missing a generation later.

Where: the map turns blue

Press Play to watch the years go by, or drag the slider. Red countries are above 2.1 children per woman, blue ones below, and the closer to gray, the closer to 2.1.

Code 
d <- df_world %>% filter(measure == "fertility", !is.na(code), year <= last_year)
lo <- 0.5; hi <- 8   # fixed colour range, so a colour means the same thing in every year
p <- plot_ly(d, type = "choropleth", locations = ~code, z = ~value, frame = ~year,
             zmin = lo, zmax = hi,
             colorscale = list(list(0, "#0082c8"), list((replacement - lo) / (hi - lo), "#f0efec"), list(1, "#E74C3C")),
             marker = list(line = list(color = "white", width = 0.3)),
             text = ~paste0(country, " · ", year, "<br>", round(value, 2), " children per woman"),
             hoverinfo = "text",
             colorbar = list(title = list(text = "children<br>per woman"), tickvals = c(1, 2.1, 4, 6, 8), len = 0.6)) %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title  = list(text = "Children per woman, by country", x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    geo    = list(showframe = FALSE, showcoastlines = FALSE, projection = list(type = "natural earth"),
                  bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    margin = list(t = 60, r = 10, l = 10, b = 170),   # room for the slider, then the source
    annotations = list(source_note(170)),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
  animation_opts(frame = 300, transition = 0, redraw = TRUE) %>%
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "Year ", font = list(size = 18, color = "gray40")))
sized(p, 600)

Interactive chart: Children per woman, by country

In 1960 almost the whole map is red: only 5 countries were below 2.1. Over the decades blue spreads, first through Europe, North America and East Asia, later through much of Latin America, North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. By 2024 the deepest red is in Africa south of the Sahara, where women in many countries still have four to six children; Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen, Iraq and parts of Central Asia are also still well above 2.1. Even there, the numbers are falling.

How fast: ten countries

The dotted line is 2.1 children per woman, the level that keeps a population steady.

Code 
paths <- c("Niger", "Nigeria", "Israel", "India", "France", "United States", "Italy", "China", "South Korea", "Greece")
highlight <- "Greece"
d <- df_world %>% filter(measure == "fertility", country %in% paths, year <= last_year)
h <- 600; b <- 110; t <- 90
p <- plot_ly()
for (cty in c(setdiff(paths, highlight), highlight)) {
  dc <- d[d$country == cty, ]
  p <- add_lines(p, data = dc, x = ~year, y = ~value, name = cty,
                 line = list(color = if (cty == highlight) "#E74C3C" else "#B3B3B3", width = if (cty == highlight) 3 else 2),
                 text = paste0(cty, " · ", dc$year, "<br>", round(dc$value, 2), " children per woman"), hoverinfo = "text")
}
ends <- d %>% group_by(country) %>% slice_max(year) %>% ungroup() %>% mutate(text = round(value, 2))
per_px <- max(d$value) * 1.1 / (h - t - b)
plotly::layout(p,
  title  = list(text = "Children per woman, 1960 to today", x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
  margin = list(t = t, r = 160, b = b),
  xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, dtick = 5, range = c(1959.5, last_year + 0.5)),
  yaxis  = list(title = "children per woman", rangemode = "tozero"),
  showlegend = FALSE,
  shapes = list(replacement_line),
  annotations = c(end_labels(ends, per_px, highlight), list(source_note(b))),
  font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
  sized(h)

Interactive chart: Children per woman, 1960 to today

The fall did not happen everywhere at the same time or the same speed:

  • South Korea went from 6 children per woman in 1960 to 0.75 in 2024, the lowest of any country with more than 10 million people. China fell from 4.5 to 1; its jagged start is the famine of 1959 to 1961, when births collapsed, and the rebound in births that followed it.
  • Italy and Greece have been below 2.1 for decades — Greece since 1981 — and are now at about 1.2. Of 217 countries, Greece has the 22nd lowest rate.
  • France and the United States stayed close to 2.1 for a long time and have only recently slipped further, to about 1.6.
  • India crossed below 2.1 around 2020. Israel is the exception among rich countries, at 2.9.
  • Nigeria and Niger are still far above, at 4.4 and 5.9, but falling.

What it does: the pyramid turns upside down

A population pyramid shows how many people there are of each age: men on the left, women on the right, the youngest at the bottom. A country with many children is wide at the bottom, like a pyramid.

Code 
pyramid_data <- function(cty, years = NULL) {
  d <- df_ages[df_ages$country == cty, ]
  if (!is.null(years)) d <- d[d$year %in% years, ]
  d$x <- ifelse(d$sex == "Men", -d$value, d$value)   # men to the left of the middle
  d$label <- paste0(d$sex, " ", d$age, " · ", d$year, "<br>", round(d$value, 1), "% of all ", tolower(d$sex))
  d
}
# x axis in % either side of the middle, labelled without the minus sign
pyramid_axis <- function(m) {
  ticks <- seq(-floor(m / 5) * 5, floor(m / 5) * 5, by = 5)
  list(title = "% of men (left) and of women (right)", range = c(-m, m),
       tickvals = ticks, ticktext = paste0(abs(ticks), "%"), zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "gray")
}
left <- "Nigeria"; right <- "Greece"
pair <- pyramid_data(left, last_year) %>% bind_rows(pyramid_data(right, last_year))
m <- max(pair$value) * 1.1
one <- function(cty, legend) {
  dc <- pair[pair$country == cty, ]
  plot_ly(dc, x = ~x, y = ~age, color = ~sex, colors = c(Men = "#0082c8", Women = "#E74C3C"),
          type = "bar", orientation = "h", text = ~label, hoverinfo = "text", textposition = "none",
          legendgroup = ~sex, showlegend = legend) %>%
    plotly::layout(xaxis = pyramid_axis(m))
}
b <- 150
p <- subplot(one(left, TRUE), one(right, FALSE), shareY = TRUE, titleX = TRUE, margin = 0.03) %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title  = list(text = paste0(left, " and ", right, " in ", last_year, ": share of the population in each age group"),
                  x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    barmode = "overlay", bargap = 0.1,
    margin = list(t = 110, b = b),
    yaxis  = list(title = "age"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.5, xanchor = "center", y = 1.08),
    annotations = list(
      list(text = paste0("<b>", left, "</b>"), x = 0.24, y = 1.0, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "center", yanchor = "bottom", showarrow = FALSE),
      list(text = paste0("<b>", right, "</b>"), x = 0.76, y = 1.0, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "center", yanchor = "bottom", showarrow = FALSE),
      source_note(b)),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25"))
sized(p, 560)

Interactive chart: Nigeria and Greece in 2024: share of the population in each age group

Nigeria, at 4.4 children per woman, is still a pyramid: the youngest group is the biggest. Greece, below 2.1 for more than forty years, has more people in their fifties than in any other group and fewer children under five than people in their seventies. People aged 65 and over are 24% of Greece’s population, children under 15 only 13%.

What the charts show

Code 
peaks <- df_world %>%
  filter(measure == "population", country %in% c("China", "South Korea", "Italy", "Greece"), year <= last_year) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(peak_year = year[which.max(value)],
            peak      = round(max(value) / 1e6, 1),
            now       = round(value[year == last_year] / 1e6, 1)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
peaks
      country peak_year   peak    now
1       China      2021 1412.4 1409.0
2      Greece      2010   11.1   10.4
3       Italy      2014   60.3   59.0
4 South Korea      2020   51.8   51.8
  • More than half the world is below 2.1: 119 of 217 countries in 2024, against 5 in 1960.
  • Countries are getting older: 53 countries now have more people over 65 than children under 15; in 1960 there was 1.
  • Some populations have started to shrink: the table above shows when the population peaked in four of them. Greece’s population peaked in 2010, Italy’s in 2014, South Korea’s in 2020 and China’s in 2021.
  • A low rate does not shrink a country at once. The large generations born earlier are still having children, people live longer, and people move in from other countries. Many countries below 2.1 are still growing; but without immigration, a rate below 2.1 for long enough means fewer people.
  • Caveats: the fertility rate is an estimate built from birth registrations, censuses and surveys, and the latest years are often projections that are revised later, especially where births are not all registered. The 2.1 level is for countries where few children die; where more die young, a population needs a little more.

Customising it

Highlight a different country

Code 
highlight <- "China"   # then re-run the "countries" chunk

A different country’s pyramid

R/mfi_fertility.rds has the age groups for South Korea, Nigeria, Greece, China, Italy and Niger:

Code 
left <- "South Korea"; right <- "Italy"   # then re-run the rest of the "pyramid_pair" chunk

For every other country, install golemworldbank (see Packages) and use its full mfi; its app also has a population pyramid tab:

library(golemworldbank)   # replaces mfi <- readRDS(...)
golemworldbank::run_app()

Further reading

  • golemworldbank — the R package and Shiny app this story’s data comes from (documentation)
  • World Development Indicators — the World Bank’s database behind mfi
  • UN World Population Prospects — where the World Bank’s fertility and age figures come from
  • Greece Since 2000 and Same Crisis, Different Endings — the other golemworldbank data stories

Rendered with R 4.6.1 · plotly · golemworldbank

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
item.description: Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Cyprus and Italy after the euro crisis, compared on income, jobs, investment, exports and people with World Bank data.
item.content:encoded:
Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Cyprus and Italy after the euro crisis, compared on income, jobs, investment, exports and people with World Bank data.

What is this?

Between 2010 and 2013 six euro countries ran into deep trouble: Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Cyprus and Italy. Five of them needed rescue loans from the other euro countries, and all six went through years of cuts and lost jobs. They started from the same crisis, but they did not end up in the same place: in 2024 the average person in Ireland produced almost twice as much as in 2008, while in Greece it was still less than in 2008.

This data story compares the six countries, in plain words, on:

  • borrowing — how much more each country bought from abroad than it sold, before the crisis,
  • income — how much the country produces per person,
  • jobs — how many people who want work cannot find it,
  • investment — what the country spends on its future,
  • exports — how much it sells to the rest of the world,
  • people — whether its population grew or shrank.

Greece is in red throughout and the other five in gray. It follows on from Greece Since 2000, which tells the Greek story on its own. All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators; the page carries its own copy of the data for these six countries and of the one function it uses, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "plotly"))
# The data and indicator_change() come from golemworldbank, copied next to this page:
# R/code_golemworldbank.R (sourced above) and R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds. For every country,
# install golemworldbank itself; its data is in Git LFS, so install it from a clone
# (install_github() can download LFS pointer files instead of the data):
#   git lfs install
#   git clone https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank.git
# then in R:
#   devtools::install_local("golemworldbank")
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)          # interactive charts

The data

golemworldbank ships the World Bank’s World Development Indicators as one long table, mfi: one row per country, indicator and year. R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds holds its rows for the six countries from 2000 onwards, every indicator. We keep the indicators this story needs, each with a short name:

Code 
# golemworldbank's mfi, six countries from 2000 (with the package installed, its mfi has every country)
mfi <- readRDS(paste0(directory, "R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds"))
countries <- c("Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Cyprus", "Italy")
last_year <- 2024   # the latest year with complete numbers: 2025 is still incomplete
indicators <- c(
  income             = "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  income_gni         = "GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  unemployment       = "Unemployment, total (% of total labor force) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  youth_unemployment = "Unemployment, youth total (% of total labor force ages 15-24) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  investment         = "Gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP)",
  current_account    = "Current account balance (% of GDP)",
  exports            = "Exports of goods and services (% of GDP)",
  population         = "Population, total"
)
df_peers <- mfi %>%
  filter(`Country Name` %in% countries, `Indicator Name` %in% indicators) %>%
  mutate(country = `Country Name`,
         year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         measure = names(indicators)[match(`Indicator Name`, indicators)]) %>%
  select(country, measure, year, value) %>%
  arrange(country, measure, year)
head(df_peers, 12)
   country         measure year      value
1   Cyprus current_account 2000  -4.887475
2   Cyprus current_account 2001  -3.099168
3   Cyprus current_account 2002  -3.320125
4   Cyprus current_account 2003  -2.007671
5   Cyprus current_account 2004  -4.773275
6   Cyprus current_account 2005  -5.266826
7   Cyprus current_account 2006  -6.367948
8   Cyprus current_account 2007  -7.636691
9   Cyprus current_account 2008 -14.385541
10  Cyprus current_account 2009  -6.670743
11  Cyprus current_account 2010 -10.762276
12  Cyprus current_account 2011  -2.093436

Each row is one country, one indicator, one year:

Column Description
country Country name
measure Short name of the indicator (the names of indicators above)
year Year of observation
value The World Bank’s value for that country and year

A few of these need a word of explanation:

  • Income (GDP per person) is the value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by the number of people who live there, in US dollars with price rises removed, so that years can be compared fairly. It is a rough measure of how well off the average person is.
  • Borrowing from abroad (the current account) is what a country earns from the rest of the world minus what it pays to it, as a share of everything it produces. A minus means it bought more than it sold and borrowed to pay the difference.
  • Investment is the money spent on things that help a country earn more later: new buildings, factories, machines, roads and equipment, as a share of everything the economy produces.

Every chart shades the euro crisis (2008 to 2013) and COVID (2020), and writes each country’s latest value at the end of its line; labels that would overlap are moved apart and joined to their line:

Code 
# a measure's value for one country and year, and the change between two values
at <- function(m, cty, y) df_peers$value[df_peers$measure == m & df_peers$country == cty & df_peers$year == y]
change_pct <- function(from, to) round((to - from) / from * 100)
big <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")
# Greece in red, the others in gray (as in the Greek Wages and Housing races)
highlight <- "Greece"
colour_of <- function(cty) ifelse(cty == highlight, "#E74C3C", "#B3B3B3")
shocks <- list(list(from = 2008,   to = 2013,   label = "Euro crisis"),
               list(from = 2019.5, to = 2020.5, label = "COVID"))
# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}
# data source as a footnote inside each chart, at the bottom of the bottom
# margin `b` (in pixels), so it lands in the same place whatever the height
source_note <- function(b) {
  list(text = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, via <a href='https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank'>golemworldbank</a>",
       xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
       xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
       font = list(size = 11, color = "#7F7F7F"))
}
# end labels: each sits right of its line's last point; labels closer than
# `gap` pixels are pushed upwards and joined to their point by a leader line.
# `per_px` is how many y units one pixel of the plot is worth
end_labels <- function(ends, per_px, unit, gap = 17) {
  o <- order(ends$value)
  y <- ends$value[o]
  for (i in seq_along(y)[-1]) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + gap * per_px)
  ends$label_y[o] <- y
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(ends)), function(i) {
    name <- if (ends$country[i] == highlight) paste0("<b>", ends$country[i], "</b>") else ends$country[i]
    list(x = ends$year[i], y = ends$value[i], xref = "x", yref = "y",
         ax = 24, ay = -(ends$label_y[i] - ends$value[i]) / per_px,
         showarrow = TRUE, arrowhead = 0, arrowwidth = 1, arrowcolor = "#B3B3B3",
         xanchor = "left", text = paste0(name, " ", ends$text[i]),
         font = list(size = 12, color = "#404040"))
  })
}
# one line per country, Greece drawn last so it sits on top. `index_year`
# turns each line into "that year = 100"; `ref` draws a dotted reference line
peer_chart <- function(m, title, ytitle, unit = "", index_year = NULL, ref = NULL,
                       tozero = TRUE, h = 520) {
  d <- df_peers[df_peers$measure == m & df_peers$year >= 2000 & df_peers$year <= last_year, ]
  if (!is.null(index_year)) {
    d <- d %>% group_by(country) %>%
      mutate(value = value / value[year == index_year] * 100) %>% ungroup()
  }
  fmt <- function(v) if (unit == "$") paste0("$", big(v)) else paste0(round(v, 1), unit)
  p <- plot_ly()
  for (cty in c(setdiff(countries, highlight), highlight)) {
    dc <- d[d$country == cty, ]
    p <- add_lines(p, data = dc, x = ~year, y = ~value, name = cty,
                   line = list(color = colour_of(cty), width = if (cty == highlight) 3 else 2),
                   text = paste0(cty, " · ", dc$year, "<br>", fmt(dc$value)), hoverinfo = "text")
  }
  ends <- d %>% filter(!is.na(value)) %>% group_by(country) %>% slice_max(year) %>% ungroup() %>%
    mutate(text = fmt(value))
  b <- 110
  lo <- if (tozero) min(0, d$value, na.rm = TRUE) else min(d$value, na.rm = TRUE)
  per_px <- (max(d$value, na.rm = TRUE) - lo) * 1.1 / (h - 90 - b)
  shapes <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(type = "rect", xref = "x", yref = "paper", x0 = s$from, x1 = s$to, y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
         fillcolor = "#EBEBEB", line = list(width = 0), layer = "below")
  })
  if (!is.null(ref)) {
    shapes <- c(shapes, list(list(type = "line", xref = "paper", x0 = 0, x1 = 1, y0 = ref, y1 = ref,
                                  line = list(dash = "dot", color = "gray"))))
  }
  tags <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(x = (s$from + s$to) / 2, y = 1, xref = "x", yref = "paper", yanchor = "bottom",
         text = s$label, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 12, color = "#666666"))
  })
  plotly::layout(p,
    title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(t = 90, r = 150, b = b),
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, range = c(1999.5, max(d$year) + 0.5)),
    yaxis  = list(title = ytitle, ticksuffix = if (unit == "%") "%" else "",
                  rangemode = if (tozero) "tozero" else "normal"),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    shapes = shapes,
    annotations = c(tags, end_labels(ends, per_px, unit), list(source_note(b))),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "#404040")) %>%
    sized(h)
}
# one bar per country, largest at the top, Greece in red; a negative bar
# carries its value inside, where it cannot run into the country names
ranked_bars <- function(values, title, h = 380) {
  d <- data.frame(country = names(values), value = unname(values))
  d <- d[order(d$value), ]
  b <- 80
  plot_ly(d, x = ~value, y = ~factor(country, levels = country), type = "bar", orientation = "h",
          marker = list(color = colour_of(d$country)),
          # rounding first (+ 0 turns -0 into 0) so -0.3 reads "+0%", never "-0%"
          text = sprintf("%+.0f%%", round(d$value) + 0),
          textposition = ifelse(d$value < 0, "inside", "outside"),
          textfont = list(color = ifelse(d$value < 0, "white", "#404040")), cliponaxis = FALSE,
          hovertext = paste0(d$country, ": ", sprintf("%+.1f%%", d$value)), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
    plotly::layout(
      title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.95, yanchor = "top"),
      margin = list(t = 70, r = 60, b = b, l = 90),
      xaxis  = list(title = "", ticksuffix = "%", zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "gray"),
      yaxis  = list(title = ""),
      annotations = list(source_note(b)),
      font   = list(size = 13, color = "#404040")) %>%
    sized(h)
}

Before the crisis: living on borrowed money

Code 
peer_chart("current_account",
           title  = "Buying more from abroad than selling (-) or less (+), % of the economy",
           ytitle = "% of the economy", unit = "%", ref = 0, tozero = FALSE)

Interactive chart: Buying more from abroad than selling (-) or less (+), % of the economy

In the 2000s borrowing was cheap across the euro area, and for years Greece, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus bought far more from the rest of the world than they sold, borrowing the difference. In 2008 the gap was -14.6% of everything Greece produced, -14.4% in Cyprus and -11.9% in Portugal. When the 2008 financial crisis made lenders nervous, the money stopped coming, and each country had to close the gap fast. By 2013 every one of them was close to zero. Italy borrowed little from abroad and Ireland less than the others: their problems came from a government that already owed a lot (Italy) and from banks that had lent too much on houses (Ireland).

Five of the six then needed rescue loans from the other euro countries, the International Monetary Fund or both, and in return had to cut spending and raise taxes:

Country Rescue Ended
Greece three loans, 2010, 2012 and 2015 2018
Ireland 2010 2013
Portugal 2011 2014
Spain a loan to rescue its banks, 2012 2014
Cyprus 2013, which also took money from large bank deposits 2016
Italy none —

Income: from almost double to still below

To compare countries of different sizes, each line starts at 100 in 2008: 110 means 10% more than in 2008, 90 means 10% less.

Code 
peer_chart("income", index_year = 2008, ref = 100, tozero = FALSE,
           title  = "Income per person, 2008 = 100 (price rises removed)",
           ytitle = "2008 = 100")

Interactive chart: Income per person, 2008 = 100 (price rises removed)

Code 
income_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) change_pct(at("income", cty, 2008), at("income", cty, 2024)))
ranked_bars(income_change, "Income per person: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)")

Interactive chart: Income per person: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)

All six fell into the crisis, but they came out of it at very different speeds. By 2024 income per person was +91% in Ireland against 2008, +19% in Cyprus, +13% in Portugal, +8% in Spain and +3% in Italy. Greece is the only one still below 2008, at -10%: its fall was the deepest and its rescue the longest.

Ireland’s numbers need a second look

Ireland’s line shoots up from 2015 because of how GDP is counted. GDP includes everything produced in the country, and many large international companies have made Ireland the base of their business for tax reasons, so their profits count as Irish production. Much of that money goes back to the companies’ owners abroad. GNI subtracts it and counts only the income that stays with people in Ireland:

Code 
d <- df_peers %>%
  filter(country == "Ireland", measure %in% c("income", "income_gni"), year <= last_year, !is.na(value)) %>%
  mutate(what = ifelse(measure == "income", "GDP per person (everything produced)", "GNI per person (income that stays)"))
p <- plot_ly(d, x = ~year, y = ~value, color = ~what, colors = c("#0082c8", "#E74C3C"),
             type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", marker = list(size = 7),
             text = ~paste0("Ireland · ", year, "<br>", what, ": $", big(value)), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
  plotly::layout(title  = list(text = "Ireland: what is produced and what stays (US$ per person, price rises removed)",
                               x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
                 margin = list(t = 80, b = 150),
                 xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90),
                 yaxis  = list(title = "US$ per person", rangemode = "tozero"),
                 legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
                 annotations = list(source_note(150)),
                 font   = list(size = 13, color = "#404040"))
sized(p, 520)

Interactive chart: Ireland: what is produced and what stays (US$ per person, price rises removed)

In 2024 Ireland’s GDP per person was $94,475, but its GNI per person $67,024. Even GNI is lifted by these companies, which is why Ireland’s own statistics office publishes a third measure that removes them; the World Bank does not carry it. The same companies explain the strange jumps in Ireland’s investment and borrowing lines below, such as investment of 53% of the economy in 2019, the year some of them moved patents and other intangible assets to Ireland. Ireland did recover strongly — its unemployment is among the lowest of the six — but by less than its GDP suggests.

Jobs: the deepest wound

The unemployment rate counts people who want a job and are looking for one, but cannot find one.

Code 
peer_chart("unemployment", unit = "%",
           title  = "People looking for work who cannot find it (%)",
           ytitle = "% of people looking for work")

Interactive chart: People looking for work who cannot find it (%)

In 2013, 28% of people looking for work in Greece and 26% in Spain could not find a job — more than 1 in 4. Among young people (15 to 24) it was 58% in Greece and 55% in Spain, more than half. Unemployment has fallen everywhere since, but not to the same level: by 2024 it was 4.3% in Ireland and 4.9% in Cyprus, against 10% in Greece and 11.4% in Spain.

Investment: Greece stopped building

Code 
peer_chart("investment", unit = "%",
           title  = "Investment in buildings, machines and roads (% of the economy)",
           ytitle = "% of the economy")

Interactive chart: Investment in buildings, machines and roads (% of the economy)

Investment fell in every country during the crisis. Most of them went back to around a fifth of what they produce, but Greece fell furthest — from 23% in 2008 to 12% in 2013 — and stayed there until 2019. In 2024 it was still 16%, the lowest of the six. A country that invests little for a decade has fewer new factories, machines and roads to earn from, which is one reason Greek incomes have been slowest to recover. (Ireland’s line jumps around for the reasons in the section above.)

Exports: everyone sells more abroad

Code 
peer_chart("exports", unit = "%",
           title  = "Exports of goods and services (% of the economy)",
           ytitle = "% of the economy")

Interactive chart: Exports of goods and services (% of the economy)

Code 
exports_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) round(at("exports", cty, 2024) - at("exports", cty, 2008)))
ranked_bars(exports_change, "Exports: change from 2008 to 2024 (percentage points of the economy)")

Interactive chart: Exports: change from 2008 to 2024 (percentage points of the economy)

The one thing all six did after the crisis was to sell more to the rest of the world. Greek exports went from 23% of the economy in 2008 to 42% in 2024, Portugal’s from 31% to 46%. The bar chart shows the change in percentage points: Greece’s exports grew by 19 points of its economy. Ireland’s exports are bigger than its whole economy, and Cyprus’s almost as big, because exports count the full value of what is sold, including parts that were imported first.

People: who stayed and who left

Code 
population_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) change_pct(at("population", cty, 2008), at("population", cty, 2024)))
ranked_bars(population_change, "Population: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)")

Interactive chart: Population: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)

During the crisis many people, often young and well educated, left to find work elsewhere. In the countries that recovered quickly, people came back and newcomers arrived: from 2008 to 2024 the population grew by 24% in Cyprus and 20% in Ireland. Greece’s shrank by 6%, also because Greek families have few children; Italy’s stayed about the same.

Comparing 2008 with 2024 with indicator_change()

golemworldbank’s indicator_change() compares every indicator a country has in two years — the same comparison as the app’s Change (%) tab. Running it for each country from 2008 to 2024 and keeping the indicators of this story gives one table of percentage changes:

Code 
change_2008_2024 <- bind_rows(lapply(countries, function(cty) {
  res <- indicator_change(mfi, country = cty, year1 = 2008, year2 = 2024)
  both <- rbind(res$increased, res$decreased)
  both <- both[both$Indicator %in% indicators[names(indicators) != "current_account"], ]
  data.frame(measure = names(indicators)[match(both$Indicator, indicators)],
             country = cty, change = round(both$`Change %`))
}))
change_2008_2024 %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = change) %>%
  arrange(match(measure, names(indicators))) %>%
  as.data.frame()
             measure Greece Ireland Portugal Spain Cyprus Italy
1             income    -10      91       13     8     19     3
2         income_gni     -7      70       22    10     10     4
3       unemployment     31     -37      -14     1     30    -3
4 youth_unemployment      4     -23       31     9     51    -5
5         investment    -31     -30      -11   -27    -24     0
6            exports     85      71       47    45     94    21
7         population     -6      20        1     6     24     0

Each number is the percentage change from 2008 to 2024: income -10 for Greece means 10% less than in 2008. Unemployment, investment and exports are themselves percentages, so their change is relative to the 2008 level (unemployment in Ireland going from 6.8% to 4.3% is a change of -37%). Borrowing from abroad is left out: it is a number that can be below zero, and a percentage change of a negative number, or of one that turns from a minus into a plus, has no clear meaning.

What the charts show

Code 
snapshot <- df_peers %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2008, 2013, 2024), measure %in% c("income", "unemployment", "investment", "exports")) %>%
  mutate(value = round(value, 1)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = value) %>%
  arrange(match(measure, names(indicators)), year) %>%
  as.data.frame()
snapshot
        measure year  Cyprus  Greece Ireland   Italy Portugal   Spain
1        income 2008 27449.2 23923.9 49461.2 33550.6  20014.5 27112.5
2        income 2013 22711.7 17644.9 47928.0 30330.0  18597.7 24498.6
3        income 2024 32757.5 21494.7 94475.0 34508.1  22664.0 29245.2
4  unemployment 2008     3.8     7.7     6.8     6.7      7.6    11.3
5  unemployment 2013    16.1    27.7    13.7    12.1     16.2    26.1
6  unemployment 2024     4.9    10.0     4.3     6.5      6.5    11.4
7    investment 2008    27.2    23.3    24.8    21.6     22.9    27.9
8    investment 2013    14.1    11.5    18.3    17.3     14.8    17.6
9    investment 2024    20.5    16.0    17.3    21.5     20.4    20.3
10      exports 2008    50.1    22.8    84.3    26.7     31.3    25.5
11      exports 2013    61.3    30.3   109.7    28.2     39.6    32.8
12      exports 2024    97.0    42.1   144.0    32.3     45.8    37.1
  • The same start: before 2008, Greece, Cyprus, Portugal and Spain bought far more from abroad than they sold and borrowed the difference. When the borrowing stopped, all of them had to cut back at once.
  • Different endings: from 2008 to 2024 income per person rose by 91% in Ireland (less in reality, see GNI), 19% in Cyprus, 13% in Portugal, 8% in Spain and 3% in Italy, and fell by 10% in Greece.
  • Jobs came back everywhere, but Greece and Spain still have the highest unemployment of the six: 10% and 11.4% in 2024, against 4.3% to 6.5% in the other four.
  • Investment is where Greece differs most: it has invested the least of the six every year since 2010.
  • Exports grew in all six — the one recipe every country followed.
  • People voted with their feet: the countries that recovered fastest gained population, Greece lost it.

Customising it

Highlight a different country

Code 
highlight <- "Portugal"
peer_chart("income", index_year = 2008, ref = 100, tozero = FALSE,
           title = "Income per person, 2008 = 100", ytitle = "2008 = 100")

Add a country

R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds holds these six countries only. With golemworldbank installed (see Packages), its mfi has every country: load it instead of the file and add the country to countries.

library(golemworldbank)   # replaces mfi <- readRDS(...)
countries <- c("Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Cyprus", "Italy", "Germany")

Another pair of years

Code 
recovery <- indicator_change(mfi, country = "Portugal", year1 = 2013, year2 = 2019)
head(recovery$increased)
head(recovery$decreased)

Further reading

  • Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery — the Greek story on its own, year by year
  • golemworldbank — the R package and Shiny app this story’s data and indicator_change() come from (documentation)
  • World Development Indicators — the World Bank’s database behind mfi
  • Greek Wages Race and Greek Housing Race — Greece against the rest of Europe on salaries, prices, rents and house prices
